entry.title: A Functional Representation of Credit Behavior for Probability of Default Modeling

link.title: A Functional Representation of Credit Behavior for Probability of Default Modeling

entry.content:
This paper proposes a framework for modeling probability of default via functional data analysis. By representing a series of credit variables as functions, we investigate whether intra-monthly information improves default predictability in linear models. We further show how a range of widely used variables, among them available funds, utilization rate, and overdraft, can all be derived from three quantities observed over time. Namely, 1) the type of each account, 2) the balance of the account, and 3) the size of the credit limit on the account. Retaining these quantities as continuous-time processes, rather than reducing them to monthly aggregated values, yields a continuous faithful representation of the borrower. When analyzing these three processes, we discovered that recurring events associated with the ordinal position among banking days created strong cyclical patterns. We therefore develop a relative time framework that aligns the recurring events across borrowers, ensuring that borrowers possess the same cyclical pattern, regardless of real time. We assess the framework using functional logistic regression. This approach accommodates the continuous representation while remaining closely related to a logistic regression model commonly used in credit risk practice, due to strict regulatory constraints. We show that, when equipped with an effective functional representation of transactional trajectories, the proposed model attains predictive performance on par with XGBoost while consistently outperforming logistic regression. Importantly, the model balances predictive performance of a machine learning model with the interpretability of linear default models, potentially enabling financial institutions to use the model, even under strict regulation.

entry.title: A Large-Dimensional Analysis of Least-Squares Federated Learning via Generalized Total Variation Minimization

link.title: A Large-Dimensional Analysis of Least-Squares Federated Learning via Generalized Total Variation Minimization

entry.content:
Federated learning over decentralized networks inherently trades off the suppression of local finite-sample noise through collaboration against the bias that collaboration introduces between heterogeneous nodes. We study this tension by performing a large-dimensional analysis of Generalized Total Variation Minimization with least-squares models. Using tools from random matrix theory, we show that Lipschitz observations of the global GTVMin solution concentrate in large dimensions, universally for any underlying network structure. We provide exact analytic expressions for the asymptotically precise performance under both i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. Gaussian mixture distributions on a fixed network. For the latter, these expressions quantify how regularization balances local adaptation against collaboration. Our theoretical results are confirmed by experiments on synthetic and real-world data.

entry.title: A New Perspective on Cumulative Residual Rényi Entropy

link.title: A New Perspective on Cumulative Residual Rényi Entropy

entry.content:
This paper introduces a new cumulative residual R'enyi entropy (CRRE), which addresses limitations of the existing cumulative residual R'enyi entropy. The conventional measure suffers from two primary drawbacks: its failure to converge to the cumulative residual entropy (CRE) as the order parameter approaches unity, and its lack of guaranteed positivity. Our proposed CRRE resolves these issues, offering a theoretically consistent and always nonnegative measure of uncertainty in residual lifetimes. We explore its mathematical properties, including its relationship with existing information measures. Furthermore, the concept is extended to its dynamic version, and its time-dependent characteristics are investigated. A non-parametric estimator of the proposed CRRE is developed, its almost sure convergence is established, and is validated through Monte Carlo simulation. The effectiveness of CRRE as a tool for quantifying uncertainty is confirmed through its application in chaotic theory and financial data.

entry.title: A Sociophysics Approach to Measuring Democracy in the Decision Making of a Group: Three Indices

link.title: A Sociophysics Approach to Measuring Democracy in the Decision Making of a Group: Three Indices

entry.content:
A group does not usually consult all its members before every decision. This paper develops a quantitative framework for measuring how widely members are consulted in decision making within a group. Two kinds of records are considered: the number of members consulted for each decision and the number of decisions in which each member is consulted. From these records, two participation indices are defined, and their equality is proved analytically. A third index measures the fraction of decisions for which at least a specified percentage of members are consulted. The distribution of consultation levels is described using a discrete maximum-entropy model from statistical physics. Tail probabilities are used to obtain bounds for the main participation index. This study examines aggregate survey data from two groups. Their observed characteristics are broadly consistent with the patterns found across the full survey. Using binomial and Poisson calculations, the future probability that all members will be consulted for a decision is examined. Inequality in consultation among members is examined through Lorenz curves, the Gini coefficient and a normalised Shannon participation measure. The member-decision structure is represented as a bipartite network. Controlled simulations show that the same overall level of consultation can have different distributions among the members. The framework measures both the overall breadth of consultation and how consultation is distributed among the members. It therefore provides a quantitative sociophysical description of one measurable aspect of democracy in decision making within a group.

entry.title: Amortized ratio-estimation importance sampling and localized simulation-based calibration for intractable likelihoods

link.title: Amortized ratio-estimation importance sampling and localized simulation-based calibration for intractable likelihoods

entry.content:
We consider simulation-based Bayesian inference (SBI) for the parameters of models with intractable likelihoods but tractable forward simulation. Building on Gaussian mixtures-of-experts surrogates, as a first contribution we develop a sequential procedure to estimate the posterior, incorporating an importance sampling step that introduces a locally amortized likelihood-to-evidence ratio estimator. The local amortization allows the ratio estimator to be evaluated at new parameter–data pairs from a local (data-dependent) design, without re-estimation, which is particularly convenient for our second contribution. The second contribution is localized simulation-based calibration (SBC). Localized SBC provides a graphical diagnostic of calibration over neighborhoods that are deliberately broader than the available posterior, at low additional computational cost. Rather than repeatedly running the full inference procedure for each simulated pseudo-observation, localized SBC fits the local surrogate and ratio estimator only once for each local design, and reuses them across all pseudo-observations. This approach is particularly appealing for SBI applications. We evaluate both contributions on three case studies, including a real-data epidemiological application.

entry.title: Analytically Optimal Sample Allocations for Nested Multivariate Multifidelity Control Variate Estimators

link.title: Analytically Optimal Sample Allocations for Nested Multivariate Multifidelity Control Variate Estimators

entry.content:
Monte Carlo estimation, an essential tool for quantifying uncertainty in complex scientific and engineering applications, often has unacceptably large errors when computing resources are limited and each sample requires evaluating an expensive high-fidelity model. Multifidelity control variate methods seek to increase the accuracy of Monte Carlo estimation by combining a limited number of expensive high-fidelity samples with a larger number of cheaper lower-fidelity samples. Many different multifidelity estimators have been proposed, including multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC), multifidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC), approximate control variates (ACVs), and multilevel best linear unbiased estimators (MLBLUEs). An important design choice in multifidelity estimation is the allocation of a limited computational budget among the available models to minimize estimator error. The state of the art in solving this budget allocation problem relies on numerical optimization; to date, closed form solutions have only been derived for estimator forms known to be suboptimal. In this work, we provide closed form expressions for optimal fractional sample allocations for a large class of nested multifidelity control variate estimators, in which higher-fidelity models are evaluated on a subset of the inputs that lower-fidelity models are evaluated on. Our analysis is based on reformulating nested MLBLUEs as an extended version of the MFMC estimator, and is applicable to general multivariate Monte Carlo estimation. We additionally propose a new approach for integer-valued budget allocation based on a greedy strategy used in combinatorial optimization, as well as a method for robust approximation of control variate coefficients from limited pilot samples. Two numerical examples illustrate our theoretical results and demonstrate the increased accuracy of our extended MFMC formulation relative to existing estimators.

entry.title: Annealed Lévy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics

link.title: Annealed Lévy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics

entry.content:
Gaussian diffusion models offer a practical framework for generative modeling. Denoising L'{e}vy Probabilistic Models (DLPM) introduce heavy-tailed perturbations with a fixed tail index throughout denoising. We introduce Annealed L'{e}vy Diffusion (ALD). ALD varies the stability index $\alpha(t)$ to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement. Our marginal-first formulation represents stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture. This formulation enables standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input. We study two sampling processes. ALD-renoise estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise. ALD-posterior preserves dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update. Both samplers reuse the same trained predictor with different scalar inputs. We evaluate ALD on four 2D benchmarks and an imbalanced nine-mode mixture. We also examine training efficiency and the effects of prediction perturbations on clipped Holtsmark data. Additional experiments evaluate MNIST and CelebA64 generation and CIFAR-10LT augmentation. ALD preserves local geometry on the evaluated light-tailed and manifold-structured targets.

entry.title: Approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic hybrid systems with empirically observed ergodic behaviour

link.title: Approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic hybrid systems with empirically observed ergodic behaviour

entry.content:
Piecewise diffusion Markov processes (PDifMPs) form a versatile class of stochastic hybrid systems that combine continuous diffusion processes with discrete event-driven dynamics, enabling flexible modelling of complex real-world hybrid phenomena. The practical utility of PDifMP models, however, depends critically on accurate estimation of their underlying parameters. In this work, we present a novel framework for parameter inference in PDifMPs based on approximate Bayesian computation (ABC). Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide detailed simulation algorithms for PDifMP sample paths. Second, we extend existing ABC summary statistics for diffusion processes to account for the hybrid nature of PDifMPs, showing particular effectiveness for ergodic systems. Third, we demonstrate our approach on several representative example PDifMPs that empirically exhibit ergodic behaviour. Our results show that the proposed ABC method reliably recovers model parameters across all examples, even in challenging scenarios where only partial information on jumps and diffusion is available or when parameters appear in state-dependent jump rate functions. These findings highlight the potential of ABC as a practical tool for inference in various complex stochastic hybrid systems.

entry.title: A proximal gradient algorithm for composite log-concave sampling

link.title: A proximal gradient algorithm for composite log-concave sampling

entry.content:
We propose an algorithm to sample from composite log-concave distributions over $\mathbb{R}^d$, i.e., densities of the form $\pi\propto e^{-f-g}$, assuming access to gradient evaluations of $\alpha_f$-convex $f$ and a restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) for $\alpha_g$-convex $g$, where $\alpha_g \ge 0$. The latter requirement means that we can easily sample from the density $\text{RGO}_{g,h,y}(x) \propto \exp(-g(x) -\frac{1}{2h}   y-x   ^2)$, which is the sampling analogue of the proximal operator for $g$. If $f + g$ is $\alpha$-convex and $f$ is $\beta$-smooth, our sampler achieves $\varepsilon$ error in total variation distance using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\kappa \sqrt d \log^4(1/\varepsilon))$ oracle calls where $\kappa := 1 \vee \beta/\alpha$, with $0\le \alpha_g \le \beta$ and $\alpha := \alpha_f + \alpha_g > 0$, which matches prior state-of-the-art results for the case $g=0$. We further extend our results to cases where (1) $\pi$ is non-log-concave but satisfies a Poincar'e or log-Sobolev inequality, and (2) $f$ is non-smooth but Lipschitz.

entry.title: Associating High-Dimensional Longitudinal Datasets through an Efficient Cross-Covariance Decomposition

link.title: Associating High-Dimensional Longitudinal Datasets through an Efficient Cross-Covariance Decomposition

entry.content:
Understanding associations between paired high-dimensional longitudinal datasets is a fundamental yet challenging problem arising across scientific domains, including longitudinal multi-omic studies. The difficulty stems from the complex, time-varying cross-covariance structure coupled with high dimensionality, which complicates both model formulation and statistical estimation for association discovery. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called Functional-Aggregated Cross-covariance Decomposition (FACD), tailored to analyzing associations in paired high-dimensional longitudinal datasets through a statistically efficient procedure. Unlike existing methods that are limited to low-dimensional data or rely on parametric modeling of temporal dynamics, FACD is capable of learning temporal structure by aggregating high-dimensional signals and accommodating variable selection to identify the most temporally associated features across datasets. We establish statistical guarantees for FACD and demonstrate its advantages over existing approaches through extensive simulation studies. Finally, we apply FACD to a longitudinal multi-omic human study, revealing blood molecules with time-varying associations across omic layers during acute exercise.

entry.title: Asymptotically Exact Negative Guidance of Diffusion Models via Positive-Unlabeled Learning

link.title: Asymptotically Exact Negative Guidance of Diffusion Models via Positive-Unlabeled Learning

entry.content:
Negative guidance of diffusion models generates samples that avoid an undesired condition, specified either by reference samples or by a conditional score alongside an unconditional model. Existing methods inject repulsive terms derived from local information at each sample, so the resulting sampler does not target an explicit density, and its bias cannot be systematically reduced by increasing computation. We instead present a negative-guidance method that samples from an explicit target density, which uniformly handles both reference-sample and score-based specifications and suppresses probability mass near the undesired condition with an avoidance strength that parametrizes the target density itself. Realizing this target requires estimating, at each diffusion timestep, how likely each sample is to belong to the undesired condition. We cast this estimation as a Positive-Unlabeled learning problem that admits lightweight online training along the diffusion trajectory, using condition samples as positives and diffusion particles as unlabeled data. Because the guided particles drift from the unconditional marginal, we further correct the residual mismatch via Sequential Monte Carlo, yielding a sampler that is asymptotically exact in the particle limit and that turns any existing negative-guidance method into its proposal kernel. Empirically, our method approaches the ground-truth target on Gaussian mixtures and Pareto-dominates existing methods on trade-offs between avoidance and generation quality, distributional bias, and diversity, including in an image-generation setting with a pretrained score network.

link.title: Asymptotics and finite sample bounds for prediction and smoothing in Wright-Fisher hidden Markov models

entry.content:
We study signal prediction and smoothing in hidden Markov models whose latent signal is a multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion and whose discrete-time observations are categorical. We consider a repeated-sampling regime with finitely many inspection times and large within-time samples. Under parent-independent mutation, the Bayesian predictive and smoothing laws admit exact representations as mixtures of Dirichlet distributions. We show that the one-step predictive and local smoothing laws converge in total variation to the corresponding Wright-Fisher transition and bridge laws determined by the neighboring population frequencies, thereby justifying plug-in approximations based on empirical proportions. For prediction, we derive explicit finite-sample bounds for this approximation and for bounded predictive functionals such as diversity, together with a finite-sample concentration bound for the marginal smoother. The joint posterior at the inspection times concentrates at the target frequencies and satisfies a Bernstein-von Mises limit with distinct interior and boundary regimes, with Gaussian and Gamma limits on different scales. The results allow arbitrary dependence across inspection times. A key technical ingredient is a fixed-interval tail bound for the coalescent-based dual death process.

entry.title: Bayesian Causal Forests for Zero-Inflated Continuous Outcomes

link.title: Bayesian Causal Forests for Zero-Inflated Continuous Outcomes

entry.content:
Estimating (heterogeneous) treatment effects is still challenging when the outcome is semicontinuous (i.e., exhibiting both a discrete point mass at zero and a skewed continuous distribution for positive values), despite the strong presence of this data type in real world settings. Existing methods either ignore the zero mass, impose fragile parametric assumptions, or suffer from extreme computational costs and data augmentation noise. This paper proposes Zero-Inflated Continuous Bayesian Causal Forests with Duan’s Smearing (ZIC-BCF-Smear), a decoupled two-part nonparametric estimator that fits a Probit BCF on the full sample to model participation and a Gaussian BCF strictly on the active subpopulation to model positive intensity. Subpopulation Propensity Adjustment (SPA) mitigates regularization-induced confounding within the active subpopulation, and Duan’s non-parametric smearing estimator re-transforms predictions to the response scale, bypassing the fragile scale multipliers of parametric models. A comprehensive simulation benchmark shows that ZIC-BCF-Smear matches well-specified parametric models without their assumptions and remains stable and calibrated where competitors either diverge or pathologically over-cover for nonlinear data. The method is then applied to individual-participant data from the SPECTRUM randomized phase III head-and-neck cancer trial, estimating the causal effect of assignment to panitumumab plus chemotherapy on the number of days patients spend with severe toxicity, an outcome for which a quarter of patients contribute an exact zero. Panitumumab assignment raises that burden by about ten days per patient under the trial’s own differential treatment duration, and the decoupled structure localizes the effect mainly in the positive-intensity part rather than in whether the reconstructed severe-AE burden is positive.

link.title: Bellman Conformal Inference: Calibrating Prediction Intervals For Time Series

entry.content:
We introduce Bellman Conformal Inference (BCI), a framework that wraps around any time series forecasting models and provides calibrated prediction intervals. Unlike the existing methods, BCI is able to leverage multi-step ahead forecasts and explicitly optimize the average interval lengths by solving a one-dimensional stochastic control problem (SCP) at each time step. In particular, we use the dynamic programming algorithm to find the optimal policy for the SCP. We prove that BCI achieves long-term coverage under arbitrary distribution shifts and temporal dependence, even with poor multi-step ahead forecasts. When the raw forecast intervals are approximately calibrated, we prove that BCI is near optimal for its surrogate model predictive control problem. We find empirically that BCI avoids uninformative intervals with infinite lengths under our main experimental configuration and generates substantially shorter prediction intervals when the raw forecast intervals are poorly calibrated.

entry.title: Beyond Expert Rankings: Contrast Calibration for Mixed-Precision MoE Quantization

link.title: Beyond Expert Rankings: Contrast Calibration for Mixed-Precision MoE Quantization

entry.content:
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, yet all expert weights must be stored. Mixed-precision quantization reduces this storage cost by assigning higher bit-widths to sensitive experts and lower bit-widths to resilient ones, but expert rankings alone do not determine how strongly to weight their errors. To address this gap, we propose NatScale, a contrast-calibrated allocation framework for mixed-precision MoE quantization. It uses a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based expert weights to an information-theoretic contrast target while preserving rankings. We jointly evaluate each expert’s gate, up and down configurations to estimate its output error. We then combine these errors and calibrated weights with an existing prior based on weight spectra, variance and precision decay to select configurations under a storage budget. Across three models, NatScale achieves the lowest native-to-quantized KL divergence and the highest top-token agreement in all nine settings against five allocation baselines. It also yields the lowest perplexity in seven settings. These findings highlight the importance of objective-aware precision allocation.

entry.title: Beyond Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Accelerators: Directed Evidence for Adaptive Sustainability Portfolios

link.title: Beyond Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Accelerators: Directed Evidence for Adaptive Sustainability Portfolios

entry.content:
Governments and development partners often seek Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) “accelerators” whose progress can propagate gains across human well-being, institutions, resources, and environmental priorities. Such claims require evidence on direction, timing, robustness, and trade-offs, not only network connectivity. We map directed SDG interdependence using a balanced panel of 114 countries observed annually from 2000 to 2024. Because the goal series are persistent, trending, and cross-sectionally dependent, we combine Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger non-causality tests on first-differenced series with false-discovery control across 272 directed goal pairs, and panel local projections with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors for 31 theory-derived indicator linkages. We find 84 directed linkages after correction: 40 synergies and 44 trade-offs. This dense structure does not support a universal accelerator. Driver-receiver rankings are fragile across lag orders, centrality metrics, bootstrap resampling, and alternative dependence controls; only peace and strong institutions as a net receiver and poverty reduction as an effect-size-weighted driver are distinguishable in the bootstrap screen. Two local-projection pathways are supported, both leading to lower child mortality, and the education-child-health association is corroborated in independent World Development Indicators data across 183 countries. The policy implication is not to abandon SDG integration, but to replace fixed global accelerator rankings with adaptive portfolios built around supported, time-lagged linkages and monitored constituent indicators.

entry.title: Bootstrap inference in factor-augmented regressions with weak factors

link.title: Bootstrap inference in factor-augmented regressions with weak factors

entry.content:
In this paper, we develop bootstrap methods for factor-augmented regressions with potentially weak common components, allowing signal eigenvalues to diverge at heterogeneous rates $N^{\alpha_k}$, where $0<\alpha_k\leq1$, $k=1,\ldots,r$. The regression estimator targets a rotation of the latent parameter vector that may be data dependent, while factor estimation can induce asymptotic bias. The proposed procedure directly constructs the rotation-specific target in the bootstrap world, avoiding the additional randomness induced by existing bootstrap methods. Bootstrap distributional validity is established for two data-dependent targets and a signal-dependent population target, where studentization provides asymptotically pivotal statistics for both analytical and bootstrap bias-corrected estimators. The analysis also distinguishes distributional approximation relative to a data-dependent target from inference on fixed population restrictions and introduces a bootstrap diagnostic for rotation uncertainty (RU) when signal eigenvalues are close. Monte Carlo experiments show improved bias correction, gains from bootstrap distributional approximation, and demonstrate that inference distortions from small signal eigengaps dissipate quickly with $T$ for fixed targets, in contrast to the persistent distortions under random rotations. An application to excess bond return predictability illustrates the practical importance of bootstrap distributional approximation and rotation uncertainty for inference on individual factor coefficients.

entry.title: Calibration and Risk-Budgeted Decisions with System One Models

link.title: Calibration and Risk-Budgeted Decisions with System One Models

entry.content:
LLM workflows and agents rely on a set of binary decisions like allow/block an input, or discard/retain a retrieved document. When human deferral is unavailable, uncertain cases must still receive an action. We study System One decision scores in this setting by defaulting to a conservative fallback when uncertain, and controlling the false omission risk within the subset of inputs assigned the utility-maximizing action. Across six datasets covering moderation, safety, and reranking, we compare general System One models with task baselines and a local open-weights fine-tuned System One model. We show that naive baselines for threshold selection exceed the target risk in roughly half of settings with defined test risk, compared with 7.8\% for Learn Then Test (LTT), which leverages finite-sample statistical guarantees. Our results show why relying on a probability-like interface is insufficient for deployment decisions and how risk-budgeted selection trades useful action against observed error.

entry.title: Change-point detection in variance-covariance matrix

link.title: Change-point detection in variance-covariance matrix

entry.content:
We consider the joint estimation of change-point locations and the sparsity pattern of the variance-covariance matrix, which is assumed to evolve in a piecewise constant manner. By applying Group Fused LASSO and LASSO penalties to the squared Frobenius norm, we estimate both the covariance structure and the change points. Adaptive weights are incorporated into the penalty terms to enhance change-point detection and covariance estimation accuracy. We establish the conditions under which the estimated change points and the sparse estimators within each segment are consistent. To solve the resulting optimization problem efficiently, we develop an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) whose updates reduce to computationally tractable subproblems. The performance of the proposed method is illustrated through synthetic and real-data experiments, including comparisons with several competing procedures.

entry.title: Common Signals, Spurious Cross-Excitation, and Identification in Multivariate Hawkes Processes

link.title: Common Signals, Spurious Cross-Excitation, and Identification in Multivariate Hawkes Processes

entry.content:
Multivariate Hawkes models are widely used to measure endogenous interactions in event data, but latent common signals can generate apparent excitation even without structural interaction. We characterize the resulting linear projection and construct stable, nonnegative Hawkes processes that share the mean intensity and Bartlett spectrum of common-signal models despite having different excitation mechanisms. This establishes a concrete form of second-order non-identification. We derive integrated third-order cumulants for Hawkes processes with Cox immigration and establish generic local identification of normalized structural parameters in two- and three-dimensional systems. An exact-equivalence Monte Carlo experiment demonstrates how third-order information can distinguish mechanisms with identical second-order structure, while revealing substantial finite-sample limitations under weak signals. For a restricted parametric family, we develop Whittle estimation from binned counts, establish consistency and asymptotic normality under appropriate identification conditions, and construct feasible sandwich standard errors accounting for estimated mean intensities. Simulations assess structural recovery and inference accuracy. An application to cryptocurrency transactions illustrates the sensitivity of inferred excitation to model specification and the limitations of structural interpretation based on spectral fit alone.

entry.title: Comparing SGLD and a fixed-noise predictor-corrector adaptation in canonical joint energy-based models on CIFAR-10

link.title: Comparing SGLD and a fixed-noise predictor-corrector adaptation in canonical joint energy-based models on CIFAR-10

entry.content:
Joint Energy-Based Models (JEM) unify classification and generation within a single network and support out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. Canonical JEM training relies on stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD); a theoretically motivated alternative, the Predictor-Corrector (PC) sampler, has not previously undergone a systematic replication test on the canonical model. We reproduce canonical JEM on WideResNet-28-10 without normalisation layers on two independent runs and test a fixed-noise PC adaptation - with the degenerate annealed-noise predictor replaced by a deterministic gradient step - across three protocols: the adapted sampler replacing SGLD throughout the full training trajectories (115-132 epochs); cold-start generation (FID); and refinement-style multi-OOD detection (AUROC). The reconstruction reaches 92.88% test accuracy and buffer-FID 44.46 (canonical: 92.90% and 38.40). We document two failure modes: catastrophic late-training divergence with the signature of the canonical outlier-buffer mechanism (all four runs), and run-dependent SVHN OOD-discrimination dynamics. No consistent method-level advantage of the adaptation over SGLD is observed on any protocol: refinement AUROC differences stay below 0.007 across ten checkpoint-OOD pairs; seeded cold-start generation favours SGLD by about five FID points; on the training protocol a hierarchical seed-by-image bootstrap gives a 95% confidence interval on the macro-averaged AUROC difference that contains zero, while a seed-level equivalence test with two runs per method cannot establish formal equivalence. The training-protocol data are consistent both with equivalence and with a small directional effect. This outcome is consistent with theory: the guarantees of the annealed-noise PC framework do not transfer to the constant-noise regime of canonical JEM.

entry.title: Compound p-values for competition-based testing

link.title: Compound p-values for competition-based testing

entry.content:
Standard competition-based multiple testing methods – such as the knockoff filter and the target-decoy procedure – are typically formulated as head-to-head competitions between a test unit and its assigned negative control unit. Motivated by real-world applications, which leverage any available negative controls, we study this competition-based framework in more intricate settings where competitions vary in size and structure. We propose new methods based on compound p-values – p-values that are superuniform only on aggregate – that enable powerful multiple testing with broader competition structures, via the Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures. The former provides exact familywise error rate control, whereas the latter may incur a false discovery rate inflation factor, for which we derive upper bounds across a range of settings. We showcase the performance of our general competition-based testing methodology through extensive simulations and real-data applications, including analyses of virtual spatial transcriptomics and CRISPR screen datasets that exhibit precisely the complex competition structures that motivate our methods.

entry.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models

link.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models

entry.content:
Compartment models of infectious diseases are often linear in coefficients that are physical parameters or products or ratios of them. We exploit this with closed-form least squares and equip the estimates with distribution-free uncertainty. Physics-informed regression (PIR) fits the parameters to finite-difference derivatives of the data; we introduce physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), which integrates the model in time instead, needs no derivatives of the data, estimates the initial state jointly and is high-order accurate. To quantify uncertainty we wrap both estimators in split conformal prediction, with a calibration population generated by the physics-based model itself, giving simultaneous intervals for all parameters with a finite-sample coverage guarantee. A residual-adaptive factor, computed without ground truth, scales the intervals to each data set (PIWR-RACC). On the eleven benchmark models of disease-informed neural networks (DINNs), PIWR or PIR-FD6 is one to four orders of magnitude more accurate than the reported DINN results wherever the sampling resolves the dynamics, in about a millisecond per fit instead of minutes to hours of training, and the 90% intervals achieve 87-92% coverage in all 88 settings. On the S3I3R model of the original PIR study, PIWR lowers the reported PIR errors by about three orders of magnitude. On real data from the 1978 boarding-school influenza outbreak, a variable-projection variant gives calibrated 95% intervals that overlap those of a Bayesian analysis. On a time-varying transmission benchmark, a B-spline expansion of beta(t) keeps PIR and PIWR linear; they are more accurate than physics-informed neural networks in three of four cases and comparable in the noisiest, with simultaneous bands for beta(t). The complete conformal calibration takes less than two minutes for every benchmark.

entry.title: Controlling the false discovery rate in high-dimensional linear models using model-X knockoffs and $p$-values

link.title: Controlling the false discovery rate in high-dimensional linear models using model-X knockoffs and $p$-values

entry.content:
We propose a novel multiple testing methodology for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) in high-dimensional linear models that integrates model-X knockoff techniques with debiased penalized regression estimators. At the foundation of our methodology, we construct and study two sets of naturally paired high-dimensional test statistics and the associated $p$-values for evaluating the same null hypotheses. The first set is shown to be asymptotically mutually independent, justifying the use of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. We further exploit the pairing structure through a two-step procedure aimed at improving power. Our theoretical results establish the key properties of the framework with respect to asymptotic FDR control and formally characterize the associated power gains of the two-step procedure. Importantly, our framework accommodates general dependence in the design matrix. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our methods outperform existing approaches – particularly those relying on empirical FDP estimates – in both power and FDR control accuracy, with notable gains in settings involving weaker signals, small sample sizes, or low target FDR levels.

entry.title: Convergence Rates of Gaussian Process Thompson Sampling for Efficient Global Optimization

link.title: Convergence Rates of Gaussian Process Thompson Sampling for Efficient Global Optimization

entry.content:
Efficient global optimization aims to identify a global optimum of an expensive black-box function within a limited evaluation budget $N$. We investigate the convergence rates of Gaussian process Thompson sampling (GP-TS) under noiseless observations, assuming a fixed objective function in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). For Mat'ern kernels with smoothness parameter $ u$ in dimension $d$, we establish a worst-case expected simple-regret upper bound of $O(N^{- u/d}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both discrete GP-TS on sufficiently fine grids and its continuous counterpart. For the continuous implementation, we develop a nested-grid argument to control posterior sample paths over the entire domain. We further establish matching lower bounds of $\Omega(N^{-5/2}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both implementations under a fixed one-dimensional Mat'ern-$5/2$ kernel, demonstrating that the logarithmic penalty is intrinsic to standard GP-TS in this setting. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Gaussian Process Capped Thompson Sampling (GP-CTS), which caps posterior sample paths using a valid RKHS norm upper bound while preserving optimism. This modification successfully eliminates the logarithmic penalty and achieves the minimax-optimal rate $\Theta(N^{- u/d})$ for both discrete and continuous implementations.

entry.title: Delay Complexity Dimension: Learning with Delayed and Censored Labels

link.title: Delay Complexity Dimension: Learning with Delayed and Censored Labels

entry.content:
We study PAC learning of binary classifiers when labels arrive after random delays and are censored beyond an observation window $W$. How many samples does this observation model require? We propose a distribution-dependent answer, the Delay Complexity Dimension (DCD). The DCD combines the VC dimension with the exact label-information rate of the observation channel. Every learner needs $\Omega(\mathrm{DCD}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. An oracle pseudo-label ERM matches this rate on the instance family of the lower bound, up to constants and logarithmic factors. On that family the DCD is within a constant factor of the classical censored-ERM complexity, and whether the DCD rate is achievable where the two separate remains open. The theory also yields a quantization scheme under which delay information lowers the residual label variance, an expedition policy with a $(1-1/e)$ guarantee for its version-space objective, and a phenomenon with no analogue in the no-delay setting. Under a fixed collection horizon, a moderate window can strictly beat immediate labels. Experiments on synthetic data and the Criteo conversion logs support these predictions. A budget-matched test of a companion labeler-diversity prediction is reported as a negative result.

entry.title: Density Discontinuity Regression

link.title: Density Discontinuity Regression

entry.content:
Many policies hinge on a continuous variable exceeding a threshold, prompting strategic behavior by agents to stay on the favorable side. This creates density discontinuities at cutoffs, evident in contexts like taxable income, corporate regulations, and academic grading. Existing methods detect these discontinuities, but systematic approaches to examine how they vary with observable characteristics are lacking. We propose a novel, interpretable Bayesian framework that jointly estimates both the log-density ratio at the cutoff and the local shape of the density, as functions of covariates, within a data-driven window. entry.title: Discrete Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Under Sparsity

link.title: Discrete Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Under Sparsity

entry.content:
Discrete diffusion models have emerged as a leading alternative to autoregressive models for generating text and other categorical data, yet their theoretical foundations remain less developed than those of their continuous counterparts. For continuous diffusion models, a prominent line of theory suggests that these models can adapt to low-dimensional structure in the data, thereby improving statistical efficiency and generalization. In this work, we investigate the discrete analogue of this phenomenon by studying the statistical rates of discrete diffusion models under sparsity assumptions. By analyzing a nonparametric estimator derived from a regularized score-entropy objective, we establish minimax-optimal rates in the sparse regime. The proposed regularization can be viewed as an adaptation of label smoothing techniques introduced for classification, and does not require the knowledge of the sparsity parameter. This shows that discrete diffusion models can adapt intrinsically to sparsity.

link.title: Discrete p-Fold Directional Models for Binned Orientation Data with Applications to Sand-Grain Orientations and Urban Street Networks

entry.content:
Discrete directional data exhibiting p-fold rotational symmetry, where directions separated by integer multiples of 2{\pi}/p are equivalent, arise in various applications but are often modeled using continuous distributions. In this article, we develop two general methods for constructing distributions for such data: symmetrization and folding of discrete circular distributions, and wrapping of discrete linear distributions. Particular models arising from these constructions are studied, together with their properties and estimation methods. For axial sand-grain orientation data, the proposed models are compared with discretized continuous axial distributions, whose category probabilities require numerical integration. The proposed models attain smaller Akaike information criterion values among the models considered while allowing direct likelihood evaluation without numerical integration. The framework is also applied to binned Manhattan street-orientation data, demonstrating its applicability to higher-order rotational structures, specifically the 4-fold case.

entry.title: Efficient contextual partial monitoring with general function approximation

link.title: Efficient contextual partial monitoring with general function approximation

entry.content:
We study finite stochastic partial monitoring (PM) games with side information, a paradigm of sequential learning with partial feedback. On each round $t \in [T]$, both player and environment observe a context and player chooses an action and environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The player neither observes the outcome nor the loss; instead, they only observe a feedback symbol which is partially informative about the outcome. We utilize the Estimation-to-Decisions (E2D) meta-algorithm of Foster et al.(2021) to design E2D.PMSide, a computationally efficient framework for contextual partial monitoring, which uses an online regression oracle to efficiently estimate the outcome distributions based on historical (context, action, feedback symbol) tuples. Since the exploration rule given by the original E2D algorithm is intractable to compute, we propose two computationally efficient exploration rules that achieve optimal regret orders in $T$: in the globally observable setting, our exploration rule is based on $\epsilon$-greedy, while in the locally observable setting, our exploration rule uses inverse gap weighting (Foster & Rakhlin, 2020), which was previously only known to be effective in the bandit setting. We show that a variant of E2D.PMSide named OE2D.PMSide can be combined with offline regression oracles to give an efficient algorithm with optimal regret when the contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. We evaluate our algorithm on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, in which a learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one. We show that our method has superior performance to prior approaches.

entry.title: Embedding Geometry Shapes LLM Routing: Tracing Failure Modes and Improving Generalization

link.title: Embedding Geometry Shapes LLM Routing: Tracing Failure Modes and Improving Generalization

entry.content:
With the growing number of LLMs available, selecting which one to use for a prompt has become a key question. A large part of the routing literature relies on semantically embedding prompts into a vector space and then applying a lightweight classifier to the embedded representations. These methods perform robustly in-distribution but they struggle to generalize to unseen tasks. By studying the geometry of semantic embeddings, we trace a clear failure mode: features that determine the neighbors of unseen prompts are an unreliable proxy for LLM selection. We therefore replace the semantic embedding with the following map: we run a partial forward pass of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the prompt and use the hidden state of its last token at a deep layer as the representation. When applying kNN and other simple classifiers to this new representation, we obtain a clear result in generalization: on average across cost penalties, their performance improves. Moreover, kNN and another simple classifier that we propose outperform every evaluated semantic-embedding baseline. Our two simple methods also beat a recent SoTA hidden-states based router on RouterBench.

entry.title: Estimating Causal Treatment Effects in Placebo-Controlled Randomized Clinical Trials When High Placebo Response is Anticipated

link.title: Estimating Causal Treatment Effects in Placebo-Controlled Randomized Clinical Trials When High Placebo Response is Anticipated

entry.content:
In placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials (RCTs), the placebo response significantly modifies treatment effects and diminishes the intention-to-treat (ITT) treatment effect, $\Delta_{ITT}$. This study presents a novel two-stage framework for estimating the standardized causal treatment effect, $\Delta_{STD}$, among the ITT population, under the assumption that their placebo responses are similar to the levels of self-administering medication at home. The first stage employs a real-world, pragmatic, single-blinded placebo lead-in to measure placebo responses to levels expected during routine at-home use. This is achieved by preserving the participants’ expectations and controlling for trial-related factors that inflate the responses. In the second stage, a double-blinded randomized phase is used to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) as a function of placebo response levels and other important effect modifiers. To facilitate CATE estimation, the prognostic scores, defined as the expected placebo responses, are used for dimension reduction. The causal estimand $\Delta_{STD}$ is computed by integrating the CATE function over the distribution of the expected placebo response levels from stage one and other modifiers. We further derive theoretical values for $\Delta_{ITT}-\Delta_{STD}$ to quantify the underestimated treatment benefit due to high placebo responses. The validity and statistical performance of the proposed framework are evaluated through comprehensive simulations.

entry.title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning

link.title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning

entry.content:
Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate-value pairs $(x, u(x))$. We ask whether inputs aligned with PDE differential structure can improve learning. Through Picard iteration on mild solutions, we show that derivatives of the input appear explicitly in the solution operator, suggesting that providing derivative features should reduce the network’s implicit differentiation burden. We prove this intuition: providing derivative features improves approximation bounds from $O(W^{-(s-m)/d})$ to $O(W^{-s/d})$, where $W$ is parameter count, $s$ is input regularity, $m$ is the PDE order, and $d$ is spatial dimension. Our central finding, however, is a surprise: the optimal derivative order $\beta^*$ is strictly less than the PDE order $m$. This gap arises from a bias-variance tradeoff in spectral space that we characterize in closed form. Learning $\beta$ from data achieves automatic spectral regularization. We introduce $\partial$-NO (del-NO), for derivative-augmented neural operators, an architecture-agnostic augmentation that provides learnable fractional derivative features to any neural operator backbone. Across benchmark problems and architectures, $\partial$-NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite-sample constraints.

entry.title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $\alpha$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models

link.title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $\alpha$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models

entry.content:
Score-based generative models driven by $\alpha$-stable L{'e}vy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy-tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving $\alpha$-stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power-law targets. In p-Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy-tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power-law tails with index $\alpha$, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light-tailed. For a target with tail index $\nu$, asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling is possible precisely when $\alpha$=$\nu$. These results identify tail-index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.

entry.title: From Plato to Aristotle: Toward a General Theory of Representation Hypotheses

link.title: From Plato to Aristotle: Toward a General Theory of Representation Hypotheses

entry.content:
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that increasingly capable models converge toward a common representation. However, recent studies have shown different views on aligning representations via their neighborhoods, spanning trees, and distances. We show that these views can differ because the alignment criteria behind them sit at different points of one lattice, and we formalize this explanation as the Lattice Representation Hypothesis (LRH). Under the LRH, the convergence claimed by the PRH is agreement at the top of the lattice, whereas its evidence comes from neighbor overlap, a criterion near the bottom. The Aristotelian Representation Hypothesis (ARH) restricts convergence to local neighborhoods because calibration keeps the growth of neighbor overlap with model size but largely removes that of centered kernel alignment. We show that this removal can come from calibrating a maximum over layers, so global convergence remains open. Back into Plato’s Cave (BPC) infers coarse shared structure from the collapse of neighbor overlap on larger evaluation sets, whereas we trace it at least partly to a fixed number of neighbors covering shorter distances. We show that the spanning-tree overlap used by Structure over Geometry (SOG) mostly repeats one-nearest-neighbor overlap. The LRH also extends to independently trained models, whose training procedure and objective decide the criteria met reliably across runs. We prove this claim for the training procedure in a linear autoencoder and for the objective in a finite contrastive Gibbs model. Experiments on dozens of pretrained vision and language models and thousands of runs of both theoretical models support these conclusions. We hope this work paves the way toward a general theory of representation hypotheses, with a framework to analyze them and compare their evidence. Project page: https://eethanshi.github.io/LRH

entry.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization

link.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization

entry.content:
Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.

entry.title: GLL: A Differentiable Graph Learning Layer for Neural Networks

link.title: GLL: A Differentiable Graph Learning Layer for Neural Networks

entry.content:
Standard deep learning architectures used for classification generate label predictions with a projection head and softmax activation function. Although successful, these methods fail to leverage the relational information between samples for generating label predictions. In recent works, graph-based learning techniques, namely Laplace learning, have been heuristically combined with neural networks for both supervised and semi-supervised learning (SSL) tasks. However, prior works approximate the gradient of the loss function with respect to the graph learning algorithm or decouple the processes; end-to-end integration with neural networks is not achieved. In this work, we derive backpropagation equations, via the adjoint method, for inclusion of a general family of graph learning layers into a neural network. The resulting method, distinct from graph neural networks, allows us to precisely integrate similarity graph construction and graph Laplacian-based label propagation into a neural network layer, replacing a projection head and softmax activation function for general classification task. Our experimental results demonstrate smooth label transitions across data, improved generalization and robustness to adversarial attacks, and improved training dynamics compared to a standard softmax-based approach.

entry.title: Gauge-Invariant, Parameter-Insensitive Regularization for Potential Recovery from Flow on Directed Graphs

link.title: Gauge-Invariant, Parameter-Insensitive Regularization for Potential Recovery from Flow on Directed Graphs

entry.content:
Recovering a latent potential from observed flow on a directed graph (a discrete Poisson problem with Dirichlet boundaries) is ill-posed, and the standard fix backfires: ridge regularization shrinks toward a gauge-meaningless origin, collapsing and reversing the recovered ordering ($+0.81\to-0.42$ rank correlation against a planted ground truth). The gauge-invariant graph Dirichlet energy removes the hazard and delivers parameter-insensitivity: the estimate is stable across four orders of magnitude in $\lambda$, whereas ridge inverts the ordering for every $\lambda>0$. We prove the reduced solve is SPD and preserves dynamic range exactly where ridge collapses it, and localize absorbing boundaries from flow alone via a Poisson residual. The $H^1$ seminorm is classical; what is new is the gauge diagnosis, the parameter-insensitivity it buys, and an ablation showing the result is robust to the extraction method. On three public clickstream corpora the gauge-invariant estimate retains $28$–$41\%$ of the interior dynamic range while ridge collapses to as little as $0.2\%$. The same gauge invariance carries into graph neural networks – neutralizing the constant mode per layer prevents the oversmoothing that collapses a deep directed GCN – linking this classical inverse problem to a central question in graph learning.

entry.title: Generalized Odds for Ordinal Outcomes: A Causal Inference Framework Adjusting for Covariates

link.title: Generalized Odds for Ordinal Outcomes: A Causal Inference Framework Adjusting for Covariates

entry.content:
Background: Generalized Odds (Gen Odds) provide summaries for ordinal outcomes without requiring the proportional odds assumption. However, conventional Gen Odds compares independently drawn treatment and control outcomes and targets a population-level contrast rather than an individual-level contrast. We developed an individual-level causal formulation of Gen Odds and examined its identification. Methods: We defined the Causal Gen Odds using the joint distribution of potential outcomes and identified it under conditional independence of the potential outcomes given baseline covariates. We developed a model-based estimator using nonproportional cumulative logistic regression and introduced an odds-ratio sensitivity parameter to assess departures from conditional independence. We evaluated the estimators through simulations and illustrated them using data from the ACCORD Study. Results: In simulations, the conditional-independence estimator was approximately unbiased with 95.5% confidence interval coverage under conditional independence, but bias and undercoverage increased with residual dependence. When the sensitivity-analysis estimator incorporated the data-generating dependence parameter, bias remained below 0.01 and coverage ranged from 93.7% to 96.1% across examined settings. In the ACCORD Study, the Causal Gen Odds for right-foot pre-tibial edema was 0.909 (95% CI: 0.880 to 0.940) under conditional independence and remained stable across the examined sensitivity range. Conclusions: The Causal Gen Odds provides an individual-level estimand that complements the conventional population-level Gen Odds. This framework enables estimation of this contrast while explicitly assessing its robustness to assumptions about dependence between potential outcomes.

link.title: Generalizing Identifiability Results in Causal Discovery from Complete Data to Missing Data Settings

entry.content:
While causal discovery methods have matured for complete data, such algorithms for handling missing values remain limited. We establish general sufficient conditions under which causal graphs remain identifiable (i.e., uniquely determined from the available data distribution) under various missingness categories, including Missing Not At Random, and provide a framework to extend correctness guarantees from causal discovery algorithms for complete data to missing data settings. Our results show that identifiability of causal graphs with no unobserved confounders is preserved when (1) missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, (2) no variable directly causes its own missingness, and (3) either faithfulness holds for missingness mechanisms, or they follow generalized linear models. Guided by these theoretical results, we introduce two asymptotically correct algorithms for Additive Noise Models (ANMs) that recover the underlying causal graph and provide consistent parameter estimates.

entry.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference

link.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference

entry.content:
Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.

entry.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

link.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

entry.content:
Regression-based survey weighting connects model-based population estimation with design-based inference through equivalent weights. For nonlinear models, equivalent weights can be defined locally through the sensitivity of a poststratified population estimator. However, conventional regression models may inadequately capture nonlinear relationships and complex interactions across sparse poststratification cells. We develop a survey-weighting framework based on hierarchical Gaussian process (HGP) regression, combining structured group-level effects with kernel-based smoothing to share information across related cells. We derive Gaussian posterior prediction formulas that exploit the structured covariance representation to reduce computational costs. We also establish a uniform convergence result for the posterior predictive mean under stated regularity conditions and construct local equivalent weights by matching the first-order sensitivity of a plug-in poststratified estimand to that of a weighted average of fitted response means, with both derivatives taken with respect to the latent mean-scale vector. Simulations show that HGP achieves lower population-weighted prediction error under nonparametric structure, whereas logistic regression performs well under correct parametric specification. Additional analyses examine sample size, frame coverage, subgroup prediction, and population-mean agreement. An application to the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study illustrates the method. Overall, this work extends local equivalent-weight construction to nonparametric modeling and provides a computational framework and conditional theoretical results for survey weighting in structured, sparse populations.

entry.title: High-Probability Regret Bounds for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling

link.title: High-Probability Regret Bounds for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling

entry.content:
Feel-good Thompson sampling (FGTS) augments the posterior of vanilla Thompson sampling with an exploration term that favors reward functions with high predicted optimal values. This modification achieves minimax-optimal regret up to logarithmic factors in linear contextual bandits, but existing analyses of its two standard variants establish regret guarantees in expectation. In this paper, we derive the first high-probability regret bounds for both cumulative and current-step FGTS in contextual bandits with general realizable function approximation. Our bounds depend on the corresponding decoupling coefficients and the prior mass near the true reward function. In the $d$-dimensional linear setting, both variants satisfy $\mathrm{Regret}(T)=O\big(d\sqrt T\log(2T)+\sqrt T\log(1/\delta)\big)$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, where $T$ is the time horizon. This bound matches the dimension and horizon dependence of algorithms based on the upper confidence bounds, up to logarithmic factors. Relative to the expected-regret guarantees, the cost of controlling the regret with high probability is confined to additive terms with at most linear dependence on $\log(1/\delta)$. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors’ guidance.

entry.title: Hopformer: Homogeneity-Pursuit Transformer for Time Series Forecasting

link.title: Hopformer: Homogeneity-Pursuit Transformer for Time Series Forecasting

entry.content:
Forecasting multiple time-series with high-dimensional covariates presents a core challenge: unifying common temporal patterns while retaining meaningful series-specific information. We introduce Hopformer (Homogeneity-Pursuit Transformer), a two-stage framework that addresses this challenge. In the first stage, we perform a Sparsity Pattern Aggregation (SPA) scheme extracting a common low-variance trend that incorporates the covariates. This acts as a homogenization layer. In the second stage, a LoRA-fine-tuned Transformer models the remaining complex dependencies in the residual. Our method is theoretically grounded. We prove that SPA achieves a near-optimal bias-variance trade-off via an oracle inequality. We also provide generalization bounds for the second stage under dependent time series data. Hopformer sets a new state of the art, improving MASE by an average of 6.56% across synthetic and real-world forecasting benchmarks.

entry.title: Improved Forecasting for Multivariate Time Series using GNAR models with General Inverse Distance Weights

link.title: Improved Forecasting for Multivariate Time Series using GNAR models with General Inverse Distance Weights

entry.content:
Many multivariate time series arise on networks where relationships between variables depend on physical or more general distances. Standard vector autoregressive models struggle in such settings due to their quadratic parameter growth, while generalised network autoregressive (GNAR) models offer a parsimonious alternative by explicitly incorporating network structures. Existing GNAR formulations assume fixed weights, typically uniform or reciprocal distances, which may not reflect the true influence of distance in real systems. We introduce a novel model with general inverse distance weights (GNARID) that extends GNAR by introducing a tunable exponent parameter that controls the strength of distance penalisation. We establish theoretical results on the consistency and asymptotic normality of new GNARID estimators, including an extension to the setting where the number of nodes grows. We analyse the effect of misspecifying the exponent on forecasting error, which helps assess how much GNAR models could be improved by our tunable weights. Simulation studies confirm the theoretical properties and show measurable benefits from correct weight specification. Using the Brumadinho ground displacement dataset, we show that proper tuning of the weight exponent improves predictive performance, highlighting the practical value of flexible distance-based weighting in network time series models.

entry.title: Improving Mendelian Randomization Analysis by Instrument Borrowing from Auxiliary Outcome Traits

link.title: Improving Mendelian Randomization Analysis by Instrument Borrowing from Auxiliary Outcome Traits

entry.content:
Mendelian randomization (MR) infers causal effects of exposures on outcomes using genetic variants as instrumental variables, but existing methods remain vulnerable to bias and loss of power when instruments are invalid. We hypothesize that closely related outcome traits share a large overlap in their valid instruments for a given exposure, so that borrowing instruments across such traits can yield more robust MR inference. To operationalize this, we introduce a novel coheterogeneity statistic, together with its asymptotic theory under different paradigms that allows for a growing number of instruments as the sample size increases, to identify secondary outcome traits likely to share valid instruments with the primary trait. We then propose extensions of two popular methods, MR-Mode and MR-PRESSO, that improve inference for the primary trait by exploiting a secondary trait. Extensive simulations show that the coheterogeneity statistic has the expected finite-sample properties and that instrument-borrowing methods consistently outperform their standard counterparts, with gains increasing as the overlap in valid instruments grows. Applications to established positive and negative control hypotheses indicate improved control of type I error and increased power. We further illustrate practical utility by revisiting the long-debated hypothesis of the causal effect of vitamin D on cardiometabolic traits.

entry.title: Interactive and Robust PCA Graphics with FSDA in MATLAB

link.title: Interactive and Robust PCA Graphics with FSDA in MATLAB

entry.content:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a standard method for dimension reduction and the exploratory analysis of multivariate data, but a complete applied workflow often requires more than numerical eigenvectors and static plots. This article documents a set of routines in the FSDA toolbox for MATLAB that implements an integrated workflow for interactive and robust PCA graphics. The software contribution consists of coordinating classical SVD-based PCA, dynamic biplot scaling controlled by row and column parameters, score-distance and orthogonal-distance diagnostics, hard-trimming robust PCA through the Minimum Covariance Determinant and the Forward Search, linked brushing, geographical displays, and three-dimensional projection diagnostics. The implementation returns reproducible numerical output while also exposing graphical controls for changing biplot geometry, confidence regions, displayed labels, robust trimming levels, and linked selections. The methodology is illustrated on quality-of-life indicators for Italian provinces, where the software reveals variable groups, atypical provinces, robust and non-robust PCA structures, and geographical patterns. The emphasis is on statistical software: no new PCA estimator is proposed, but established PCA and robust-PCA methodology is combined in a documented, extensible, and script-reproducible MATLAB environment.

entry.title: Inverse Probability Weighting-based Mediation Analysis for Microbiome Data

link.title: Inverse Probability Weighting-based Mediation Analysis for Microbiome Data

entry.content:
Motivation: Mediation analysis is an important tool for elucidating causal mechanisms in biomedical research and has recently gained increasing attention in microbiome studies. Motivated by a microbiome study of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients, we investigate whether the effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection status is mediated through gut microbial taxa. This problem poses substantial methodological challenges due to the high dimensionality, zero inflation, and dependence of microbial mediators, as well as the presence of an exposure-induced mediator–outcome confounder, antibiotic use. Results: To address these challenges, we propose a novel nonparametric identification formula for the interventional indirect effect, a causal mediation estimand that remains identifiable in the presence of exposure-induced mediator–outcome confounding. Building on this identification result, we develop an inverse probability weighting estimator and construct standard normal bootstrap confidence intervals for inference. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate effect estimation and maintains appropriate type I error rates and power in finite samples. Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome. Availability and implementation: The R code for the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/YX-ZHANG-1/CausalMediationMicrobiome and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21960802.

entry.title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data

link.title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data

entry.content:
Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM” that generates the original’s reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.

entry.title: Is Flow Matching Just Trajectory Replay for Sequential Data?

link.title: Is Flow Matching Just Trajectory Replay for Sequential Data?

entry.content:
Flow matching (FM) is increasingly used in scientific domains for time series generation and forecasting, where data often arise from underlying dynamical systems. However, it is not well-understood whether it learns transferable dynamical structure or simply performs an effective ‘‘trajectory replay’’. We study this question by deriving the optimal velocity field targeted by the empirical FM objective on sequential data. For the Gaussian conditional paths commonly used in practice, we show that the resulting sampler is an ODE whose dynamics describe a nonparametric, memory-augmented continuous-time dynamical system. The driving velocity field admits a closed-form expression as a weighted mixture of instantaneous velocities determined by observed transitions. This characterization provides an interpretable view of neural FM models as parametric estimation of an underlying nonparametric target and naturally leads to FreeFM: a closed-form, training-free realization of this target. FreeFM provides a transparent reference for studying sequential FM while yielding effective probabilistic forecasts directly from historical transitions.
