entry.title: Large-Step Last-Iterate Convergence of Random-Reshuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent

link.title: Large-Step Last-Iterate Convergence of Random-Reshuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent

entry.content:
Random reshuffling stochastic gradient descent (RR-SGD) is widely used for finite-sum optimization in machine learning. For convex $L$-smooth components, recent work establishes convergence guarantees for an averaged iterate with component stepsizes as large as order $1/L$. However, the final iterate is a natural output in practice, and existing last-iterate guarantees in this setting require stepsizes that scale inversely with the number of components $n$. We establish an expected objective-gap bound for the last iterate of standard RR-SGD on unconstrained problems with a constant component stepsize satisfying $0<\eta\lesssim 1/(L(1 + \log(nK)))$, where $K$ is the number of epochs. By retaining the sampling bias at random comparison points, we remove the explicit $1/n$ factor from the stepsize restriction. Combined with existing small-step bounds, our result matches the corresponding averaged-iterate convergence rate up to logarithmic factors.

link.title: Limits of Statistical Assurance for Embodied and Agentic AI under Adaptive Adversaries

entry.content:
Finite safety assessments cannot exclude an adversary that preserves unattacked behavior until certification and activates afterward. We characterize this limitation for embodied and tool-use AI. An adversary that matches the complete observation law until observable, irrevocable certification and retains intervention access afterward attains $v\mathbb{E}[(n-S_0)_+]$ expected post-certification events over $n$ trials, where $v$ is the active event probability and $S_0$ the unattacked certification time. The result covers adaptive and privately randomized evaluators. Switching at certification is exactly optimal for a fixed likelihood-ratio test under memoryless, event-increasing interventions without a binding intervention budget. A positive clean-certification requirement forces linear worst-case expected excess when intervention raises event rates over an authorized deployment horizon, even if certification is deferred to the deadline. In simulated RoCo collaboration, switching yields commanded-separation violations in 34 of 36 post-certification episodes. Preregistered randomized AgentDojo trials estimate 1.98 additional security violations per four-task continuation (95% interval [1.67, 2.29]). An adversarial language-model controller infers hidden certification from noisy evaluation receipts and times intervention accordingly. With permanent revocation, a mixture likelihood-ratio monitor bounds cumulative excess above a prespecified reference rate at square-root order, up to logarithmic factors, on every sample path. A single fixed alternative can permit linear expected excess under stationary attacks. Against a controller observing the monitor’s rule and statistic, live mixture monitoring reduces violations from 12.00 to 3.81 per 24 assigned task opportunities. entry.title: Linear regression with probabilistic networks for network-linked data

link.title: Linear regression with probabilistic networks for network-linked data

entry.content:
Network-linked data combine a network with covariates and responses observed for its nodes. Common regression approaches either model dependence among neighboring responses using the observed network or capture similarities associated with network structure without explicitly modeling response dependence. We propose a probabilistic network-linked data analysis framework that incorporates both features while accounting for randomness in network formation. The model uses normalized connection probabilities to weight peer responses and latent positions to capture network cohesion. A two-step likelihood procedure first estimates the network structure and then fits the response model. We establish theoretical guarantees for network recovery in sparse networks with heterogeneous node effects, and prove consistency and joint asymptotic normality of the regression estimators subject to suitable conditions. The analysis also clarifies when estimating the network preserves the classical convergence rate for spatial autoregressive models. Simulation studies demonstrate the estimation performance of the method and assess its inference accuracy. An analysis of diplomatic network data illustrates its practical application.

entry.title: Living Synthetic Benchmarks: A Neutral and Cumulative Framework for Simulation Studies

link.title: Living Synthetic Benchmarks: A Neutral and Cumulative Framework for Simulation Studies

entry.content:
Simulation studies are widely used to evaluate statistical methods. However, new methods are often introduced and evaluated using data-generating mechanisms (DGMs) devised by the same authors. This coupling creates misaligned incentives, e.g., the need to demonstrate the superiority of new methods, potentially compromising the neutrality of simulation studies. Furthermore, results of simulation studies are often difficult to compare due to differences in DGMs, competing methods, and performance measures. This fragmentation can lead to conflicting conclusions, hinder methodological progress, and delay the adoption of effective methods. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of living synthetic benchmarks. The key idea is to disentangle method and simulation study development and continuously update the benchmark whenever a new DGM, method, or performance measure becomes available. This separation benefits the neutrality of method evaluation, emphasizes the development of both methods and DGMs, and enables systematic comparisons. In this paper, we outline a blueprint for building and maintaining such benchmarks, discuss the technical and organizational challenges of implementation, and demonstrate feasibility with a prototype benchmark for publication bias adjustment methods. We conclude that living synthetic benchmarks have the potential to foster neutral, reproducible, and cumulative evaluation of methods, benefiting both method developers and users.

entry.title: Log-regularly varying scale mixture of asymmetric Laplaces for robust Bayesian quantile regression

link.title: Log-regularly varying scale mixture of asymmetric Laplaces for robust Bayesian quantile regression

entry.content:
Bayesian quantile regression based on the asymmetric Laplace (AL) distribution can be sensitive to extreme observations because of its exponentially decaying tails. We propose a robust error distribution constructed as a finite mixture of the AL distribution and a log-Pareto scale mixture of asymmetric Laplace distributions (LPAL). Unlike a direct log-Pareto extension of the normal location-scale representation of the AL distribution, the proposed AL-LPAL mixture preserves the prescribed quantile and exhibits log-regularly varying behavior in both tails. The LPAL component also has an unbounded density at the target quantile, yielding a distribution that combines sharp central concentration with super-heavy tails. We establish posterior robustness under arbitrarily extreme contamination and provide sufficient conditions for the existence of posterior moments of the regression coefficients and scale parameter. For posterior computation, we develop a Gibbs sampler using latent-variable augmentations and a computationally efficient mean-field variational Bayes approximation. Simulation studies show that the proposed method is competitive under moderate contamination and maintains stable point estimation with comparatively concentrated posterior intervals, particularly when severe contamination affects the quantile of interest. Applications to carbon dioxide and Boston housing data, using the same preprocessing as existing robust Bayesian quantile regression analyses, show favorable predictive performance across nearly all quantile levels and loss criteria considered.

entry.title: Longitudinal Brain Aging in Covariance Space: Temporally Calibrated Bayesian Inference for Adaptive Covariance Operators

link.title: Longitudinal Brain Aging in Covariance Space: Temporally Calibrated Bayesian Inference for Adaptive Covariance Operators

entry.content:
Functional brain aging is often characterized by differences between people of different ages, although aging unfolds within individuals. This distinction is especially important for functional connectivity, where the direction of covariance change may evolve across adulthood. We introduce a Bayesian longitudinal covariance-operator framework that models each visit covariance as a latent positive-definite state informed by repeated resting-state fMRI runs. The approach calibrates run-level information for temporal dependence and replicate variability, separates within-person aging from between-person age differences, and uses an adaptive tangent representation to learn the low-dimensional structure of longitudinal change without relying on pooled covariance variation. The longitudinal operator varies smoothly in magnitude and orientation with age, while exact Fr'echet derivatives translate the fitted trajectory to the covariance scale. This framework allows us to examine how brain covariance organization changes within individuals, whether longitudinal aging follows the population age gradient, and which functional systems contribute to their divergence. In the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study, within-person covariance aging differs substantially from the cross-sectional age gradient through early and middle adulthood, with the discrepancy diminishing later in life. Covariance reorganization is strongest around midlife, and the longitudinal signal is concentrated in a few coordinated directions, with most off-diagonal change occurring between functional systems. These findings demonstrate that population-level signatures of brain aging do not necessarily reflect individual aging trajectories and highlight the importance of modeling longitudinal covariance change directly.

entry.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models

link.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models

entry.content:
Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model’s training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample’s likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample’s local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

entry.title: MAEM: Mitigating Recency Bias via a Replay-Free, Capacity-Controlled Dynamic Mixture of Experts for Class-Incremental Graph Learning

link.title: MAEM: Mitigating Recency Bias via a Replay-Free, Capacity-Controlled Dynamic Mixture of Experts for Class-Incremental Graph Learning

entry.content:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads—information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components. We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.

entry.title: MCMC Can See Can’t See

link.title: MCMC Can See Can’t See

entry.content:
It is folklore that passing “convergence” diagnostics does not guarantee that a Markov chain has converged. We prove this as an impossibility for any finite checklist of diagnostics. Running more chains, longer chains, and smarter diagnostics does not avoid this impossibility in certifying convergence. Under regularity assumptions, we determine how the worst-case undetected non-convergence decays as more diagnostics are added, and how to choose diagnostics optimally. Folklore suggests that the sampler’s slowest mixing modes are the “dangerous” ones that must be monitored; we prove that the slow modes yield nearly optimal diagnostics as sampling proceeds. Given a source class, we also give an anytime-valid bound on the remaining discrepancy and show how undetected bias caps the effective sample size that a finite checklist can certify.

link.title: Maximum-Entropy Exploration with Future State-Action Visitation Measures

entry.content:
Maximum entropy reinforcement learning motivates agents to explore states and actions to maximize the entropy of some distribution, typically by providing additional intrinsic rewards proportional to that entropy function. In this paper, we study intrinsic rewards proportional to the entropy of the discounted distribution of state-action features visited during future time steps. This approach is motivated by two results. First, we show that the expected sum of these intrinsic rewards is a lower bound on the entropy of the discounted distribution of state-action features visited in trajectories starting from the initial states, which we relate to an alternative maximum entropy objective. Second, we show that the distribution used in the intrinsic reward definition is the fixed point of a contraction operator and can therefore be estimated off-policy. Experiments highlight that the new objective often leads to improved visitation of features within individual trajectories, in exchange for slightly reduced visitation of features in expectation over different trajectories, as suggested by the lower bound. It also leads to improved convergence speed for learning exploration-only agents. Control performance remains similar across most methods on the considered benchmarks.

entry.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters

link.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters

entry.content:
Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

entry.title: Measuring frailty in the elderly: an indicator based on a super-classifier

link.title: Measuring frailty in the elderly: an indicator based on a super-classifier

entry.content:
Identifying frail older adults in an ageing population is essential for improving healthcare services. This study proposes a composite indicator to assess individual frailty levels using administrative healthcare data. Given the complex and multidimensional nature of frailty, a multi-outcome approach is adopted. Following an extensive literature review, a set of adverse health events is selected as proxies for frailty. These events were modelled using logistic classifiers, with frailty determinants (associated to adverse health events, selected using a gradient tree boosting) serving as covariates. The sensitivity and specificity of each classifier is used to compose their combined likelihood. From this, we derive an indicator capable of quantifying frailty across the population. The indicator shows robust performance across multiple outcomes and over time. Its primary innovation lies in allowing the use of diverse and outcome-specific sets of frailty determinants without any structural constraint. Overall, we offer an effective tool for quantifying frailty among older adults, potentially supporting health authorities in the prevention of frailty-related adverse events.

entry.title: Memory by Design: Bayesian Layers for Sequence Modeling

link.title: Memory by Design: Bayesian Layers for Sequence Modeling

entry.content:
We introduce the \emph{design-model framework}: a way to derive efficient recurrent sequence maps from explicit assumptions about memory. A design model writes evidence into memory by exact Bayesian filtering; a query- dependent readout produces a predictive distribution whose mean is the layer output. In our linear-Gaussian instantiation, the \emph{Bayesian Layer} propagates both a mean and a covariance: the covariance tracks uncertainty over stored associations, steering writes toward uncertain directions, attenuating gains as evidence accumulates, and preserving confident memories. The same framework unifies several sub-quadratic recurrences: linear attention, GLA, and Mamba-2/SSD are exact filters under a latent-input design model, whereas DeltaNet and related Delta-rule models are covariance-reset reductions of the Bayesian Layer’s design model. Restoring covariance propagation yields closed-form predictions for retrieval dynamics, which we verify empirically, and improves robustness beyond the training regime in controlled collision studies, learned associative recall, and the Zoology MQAR benchmark. Training from scratch on WikiText-103 under matched state budgets lowers perplexity on associative-recall hits. Distilling Bayesian Layers into a pretrained 340M Gated DeltaNet improves RULER long-context retrieval over a matched-compute control, at a 2.5–2.7\% held-out perplexity cost.

entry.content:
We study the minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap $\gamma_{ps}$ of a Markov chain from the observation of a single trajectory. Extending earlier works on finite-state space chains by Wolfer and Kontorovich (2024), we provide an estimator in the case of a compact, continuous state-space. Our estimator appears to be minimax-optimal on the class of chains with a transition operator with Lipschitz density, up to logarithmic terms. Our estimator, combined with Paulin’s version of Bernstein inequality, allows to derive empirical concentration inequalities for Markov chains. This unlocks many applications, from confidence intervals, to active learning and generalization bounds. In particular, for rested bandits with Markov rewards, we provide a version of UCB with a regret bound similar to the one in the iid case, without assuming any knowledge on the pseudo-spectral gap of the chains.

entry.title: Mixed Poisson diffusion models and application to posterior sampling

link.title: Mixed Poisson diffusion models and application to posterior sampling

entry.content:
Diffusion models are a powerful framework for learning complex probability distributions. While widely used diffusion models for continuous data rely on Gaussian noising processes, we instead develop diffusion models based on Poisson noise. More precisely, we introduce and study a new mathematical framework, called Mixed Poisson Diffusion Models (MPDM), with noising dynamics driven by multivariate counting processes. Our methodology is motivated by Poisson inverse problems. The success of Gaussian diffusion models has led to their use as prior models in a growing number of posterior sampling methods for inverse problems. However, most of these approaches focus on Gaussian inverse problems, in which observations are generated through a deterministic forward operator corrupted by additive Gaussian noise. By contrast, Poisson inverse problems, where observations are discrete and Poisson distributed, remain comparatively underexplored in this literature. Building on our Poisson generative dynamics, we develop a natural framework for posterior sampling in Poisson inverse problems and derive several posterior sampling algorithms based on the proposed model. We evaluate our approach on realistic Poisson inverse problems and show that the resulting framework is well suited to this class of problems.

entry.content:
Individualized survival predictions are often summarized by scalar risk scores or event probabilities at selected time horizons, although clinically relevant risk may also differ in its temporal organization. We consider finite-dimensional representations of individual hazard trajectories through interpretable hazard functionals, such as peak timing, cumulative hazard over prespecified intervals, and persistence of elevated risk. A central issue is that the richness of such representations is constrained by the hazard geometry supported by the underlying survival model. We formalize this through model-induced tangent spaces and functional ranks, derive an exact decomposition of model-supported variation into directions retained and lost by a chosen representation, and introduce a model-relative notion of local completeness. We further distinguish intrinsic model capacity from the variation actually activated by covariates. These results motivate a structured extension of AFT time scaling through a positive-affine deformation on the log-time scale, yielding a power-warp mechanism with an additional temporal deformation direction. Combined with a log-logistic reference hazard, this gives a parsimonious likelihood-based working specification for which peak timing and peak height provide complete coordinates over the unimodal regime. We also establish plug-in recovery and asymptotic inference for hazard functionals. Simulations and a lung-cancer application illustrate how model-induced restrictions propagate to hazard-functional representations.

entry.title: Multi-Sensitive Distributional Fairness: Joint Wasserstein Audits and Shapley Allocation

link.title: Multi-Sensitive Distributional Fairness: Joint Wasserstein Audits and Shapley Allocation

entry.content:
Fairness audits with several sensitive attributes are often performed one coordinate at a time. This can miss purely intersectional disparities: a score may be independent of each sensitive coordinate while depending on their joint profile. We study distributional demographic parity for a real-valued score using one-dimensional Wasserstein geometry. We distinguish two complementary constructions. Conditional and sequential audits characterize joint parity through their zero sets, but their positive values do not generally decompose a fixed joint Wasserstein disparity. By contrast, full-cell conditional quantile functions define a Hilbert-valued random variable whose variance is the joint disparity. Conditional expectations of this quantile process induce a monotone information game: every reveal order yields an exact martingale decomposition of the same joint disparity, while Shapley values provide an order-free attribution across sensitive attributes. Under independent sensitive attributes, the game reduces to a Hoeffding-ANOVA decomposition and Shapley splits each interaction energy equally among its members; under dependence, orthogonality is lost and explicit formulas reveal suppression and redundancy effects that marginal audits can hide. We give fixed-grid estimators and permutation calibration, and illustrate the framework on synthetic examples and ACSIncome. The resulting framework separates three questions that are often conflated: whether joint distributional parity holds, how a fixed joint disparity decomposes along an information path, and how that disparity can be attributed across sensitive coordinates without privileging an ordering.

entry.title: Multivariate Lévy Adaptive B-Spline Regression

link.title: Multivariate Lévy Adaptive B-Spline Regression

entry.content:
We propose Multivariate L'evy Adaptive B-Spline Regression (MLABS), a Bayesian nonparametric regression model designed to capture nonlinear effects, interactions, and locally varying features of multivariate functions. MLABS represents the regression function as a random sum of low-order tensor-product B-spline basis functions under a finite L'evy random measure prior. The resulting representation adapts to the complexity and local structure of the regression function while favoring a sparse basis representation. For posterior inference, we develop a reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm with Bayesian backfitting, collapsed trans-dimensional updates, and residual-guided proposals. These computational strategies are designed to improve posterior exploration across basis configurations of varying dimensions and structures. We also establish approximation bounds for functions with low-order interactions and heterogeneous smoothness. These bounds relate approximation accuracy to the number of basis terms. Simulation studies show that MLABS achieves competitive predictive performance across a wide range of regression settings, including high-dimensional problems. MLABS also demonstrates robust predictive performance across benchmark real datasets. In an environmental-mixture application, it attains predictive accuracy comparable to Bayesian kernel machine regression at substantially lower computational cost.

entry.title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments

link.title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments

entry.content:
Learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR) with many treatments requires estimating treatment-specific effects from limited observations per arm. Treatments with similar conditional responses can share information, but linear contrast models may miss nonlinear heterogeneity. We propose nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (NSCF), a neural Q-learning framework with a shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings. Pairwise fusion groups treatments with similar learned contrasts, yielding an ITR and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, validation-based partition selection, and unpenalized grouped refitting. NSCF lowers regret relative to a strong neural reference in nonlinear exact-sharing simulations; perturbations characterize the limits of hard sharing. In a melanoma xenograft application, NSCF improves average policy value over the neural reference. These results support nonlinear representation learning with supervised treatment fusion when treatment effects exhibit shared structure.

entry.title: Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference

link.title: Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference

entry.content:
Population dynamics are often observed only as unpaired snapshots, which leave the evolution between measurements underdetermined. Second-order regularization can constrain it, but a penalty on the accelerations of sampled particles is a prior on joint particle paths, and different particle representations of the same marginal curve can have different acceleration costs. We therefore introduce Neural Wasserstein Splines (NWSP), a sample-based method that learns a continuous population curve under a Wasserstein smoothness prior. A neural network maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come from the spline basis without numerical integration. We project the generator’s velocity onto gradients of a finite dictionary of scalar potentials and differentiate this measure-dependent projection in time, obtaining a finite-dimensional surrogate for the intrinsic Wasserstein acceleration, trained jointly with distributional fit losses. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, we prove that the population penalty depends only on the marginal curve and bound its sensitivity to moment-estimation errors. Learned potentials (NWSP-N) sharpen acceleration estimates. On various synthetic and single-cell benchmarks, NWSP is highly competitive with transport and flow-based methods, ranking in the top two in 11 of 16 settings. The penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16 settings and, while competitive with a particle-acceleration penalty, adds provable representation invariance.

entry.title: Noise-Aware Differentially Private Variational Inference

link.title: Noise-Aware Differentially Private Variational Inference

entry.content:
Differential privacy (DP) provides robust privacy guarantees for statistical inference, but this can lead to unreliable results and biases in downstream applications. While several noise-aware approaches have been proposed which integrate DP perturbation into the inference, they are limited to specific types of simple probabilistic models. In this work, we propose a novel method for noise-aware approximate Bayesian inference based on stochastic gradient variational inference which can also be applied to high-dimensional and non-conjugate models. We also propose a more accurate evaluation method for noise-aware posteriors. Empirically, our inference method has similar performance to existing methods in the domain where they are applicable. Outside this domain, we obtain accurate coverages on high-dimensional Bayesian linear regression and well-calibrated predictive probabilities on Bayesian logistic regression with the UCI Adult dataset.

entry.title: Noisy-Label Calibration with Multiple Unreliable Labels

link.title: Noisy-Label Calibration with Multiple Unreliable Labels

entry.content:
In medical annotation and crowdsourcing, multiple annotators assign labels to each example, but these labels may be incorrect. Treating such noisy labels as ground truth can bias calibration evaluation. To address this problem, we propose methods for evaluating and recalibrating a fixed binary predictor under the underlying clean-label distribution, using only noisy annotations. First, given annotator-specific noise probabilities, we propose Noise Corrected ECE (NC-ECE), a binned estimator of expected calibration error (ECE) under class-conditional noise. We derive non-asymptotic bounds on the estimator’s bias. Then, we propose practical algorithms for estimating unknown noise probabilities under conditional independence and label-orientation assumptions. We also develop loss-based and histogram post-hoc recalibration with clean-risk and calibration guarantees, respectively. Experiments on semi-synthetic benchmarks show that the proposed ECE estimator closely tracks its clean-label oracle counterpart and that the recalibration methods substantially improve latent-label calibration, whereas uncorrected recalibration against noisy annotations can degrade it.

entry.title: Non-Invariance in Nested Prediction Models under Selective Predictor Availability

link.title: Non-Invariance in Nested Prediction Models under Selective Predictor Availability

entry.content:
We used nested models as a framework for characterising the consequences of a selectively measured predictor in clinical prediction models. In this framework, a model containing predictors available in the target population is referred to as the restricted model, while the extended model additionally includes a selectively measured predictor. We show that non-invariance in the restricted model between selected patients and the target population decomposes into components due to omission of the additional predictor, potential residual non-invariance, and their interaction. This framework is extended to a predictor measured via multiple routes of selection resulting in collider structures. We further show that imputation based on the conditional distribution of the additional predictor in the selected population transfers the restricted-model non-invariance to the imputed extended model as imputation bias. In a forthcoming version, this framework will be illustrated using real world and simulated data. The framework provides a formal basis for understanding how selective predictor measurement affects generalisability of clinical prediction models using routinely collected health data.

entry.title: On Complexity of Gaussian Sampling

link.title: On Complexity of Gaussian Sampling

entry.content:
We study the number of exact matrix-vector queries needed to sample a centered $d$-dimensional Gaussian with condition number at most $\kappa$ to total variation error $\varepsilon$. The best known algorithm uses $O(\min{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\frac{d}{\varepsilon})})$ queries, while the known lower bounds do not grow as $\varepsilon\to0$ and match this bound only for $\kappa\le d^{1/5-\delta}$ at constant accuracy. We introduce a construction based on a hidden determinant sign and prove a lower bound of $\Omega!\left(\min\left{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\right)\right}\right)$ uniformly for all $d\ge1$, $\kappa\ge4$, and $0<\varepsilon\le\tfrac{1}{16}$. This bound matches the known upper bound up to constant factors whenever $\kappa\le d^{2-\delta}$ for fixed $\delta\in(0,2)$, or $\varepsilon\le d^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. We also extend a recent fixed-spectrum construction with a hidden eigenbasis from $\kappa=2$ to $2\le\kappa\le d^{1-\delta}$, for any fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$. This gives an $\Omega_\delta(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ lower bound at constant accuracy that holds even when the spectrum of the precision matrix is known to the algorithm.

entry.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization

link.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization

entry.content:
Recent work has sought to transfer first-order nonconvex optimization guarantees to zeroth-order methods through gradient estimators, typically incurring a factor linear in $d$. \citet{kornowski2024} obtained an $\mathcal{O}(d\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ oracle complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and asked whether its dependence on all three parameters is jointly optimal. Although the dimension dependence and the first-order dependence on $(\delta,\epsilon)$ are separately known to be unavoidable, a matching zeroth-order lower bound has remained open. We answer this question in the unrestricted full-space setting. For smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, we establish a scalar-oracle lower bound of $\Omega!\left(dL_0^2\min{\Delta H,L_0^2}/\epsilon^4\right)$ assuming a smooth, globally lower-bounded population objective and a second-moment bound on sample Lipschitz constants. A smooth reduction then yields a lower bound for Goldstein stationarity, proving the joint minimax optimality of the dependence on $(d,\delta,\epsilon)$ under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. Crucially, our results allow algorithms to query arbitrary points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, adaptively select sample-function labels, reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, and output points without spatial restrictions. Thus, unlike lower bounds based on bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, our guarantees apply to a fully adaptive, reusable-sample scalar oracle. We also establish a separate noiseless exact-value lower bound against randomized algorithms, and hence also against deterministic methods. Our proof combines a globally defined sequential nonconvex construction with an exact Gaussian scalar channel, multistage random-field estimates, and an antithetic finite-sample realization that preserves information hardness under adaptive reuse.

entry.title: On Inherent Privacy of Posterior Sampling: A Unified Rényi-Divergence Framework

link.title: On Inherent Privacy of Posterior Sampling: A Unified Rényi-Divergence Framework

entry.content:
Differential Privacy (DP) provides a rigorous framework for quantifying privacy guarantees. While most methods achieve DP by injecting calibrated random noise, the intrinsic randomness of certain procedures such as sampling can yield DP guarantees ``for free’’. In this work, we develop a unified R'enyi divergence framework to characterize the inherent DP guarantees of sampling from a Bayesian posterior distribution. We show that the privacy loss incurred by One-Posterior-Sampling (OPS) is governed by posterior exponential moments of the single-record log-likelihood ratio, and establish explicit DP guarantees under uniformly bounded, sub-Gaussian, or sub-exponential tail regimes. We apply the framework to representative Bayesian models, including categorical likelihoods with arbitrary priors, Gaussian-Gaussian conjugate pair, generalized linear models from the exponential family and linear regression with Gaussian likelihood, both with Gaussian priors on the regression coefficients. Our results elucidate sample size, model structure, neighboring relations in DP (bounded or unbounded), and how prior if applicable, jointly determine the inherent DP guarantees of OPS. Furthermore, our results recover the existing DP guarantees for OPS as special cases – often with tighter privacy loss bounds – and substantially broaden the class of Bayesian models for which the inherent DP guarantees of OPS can be rigorously characterized.

entry.title: On Local Inference for Functionals of Ill-Posed Inverse Problems

link.title: On Local Inference for Functionals of Ill-Posed Inverse Problems

entry.content:
We study inference for continuous linear functionals of solutions to ill-posed inverse problems, including Euclidean parameters arising in nonparametric instrumental variables, proximal causal inference, and shadow-variable models. Although pointwise root-$n$ inference is possible under standard conditions, we show that this need not translate into locally reliable inference. Under a model imposing only minimal regularity conditions, the target is Hellinger discontinuous when both inverse problems are ill-posed: arbitrarily small changes in the data-generating law can produce arbitrarily large changes in the target, ruling out informative locally uniform inference. Imposing a uniform bound on a minimum-norm solution restores Hellinger continuity under regularity conditions, but does not by itself ensure stable root-n inference. If, in addition, both inverse problems are ill-posed and the solution whose norm is uniformly bounded is nonunique at a law $P_0$, then under regularity conditions the target fails to be pathwise differentiable; consequently, asymptotically linear estimators exhibit nonvanishing root-$n$ bias under some local alternatives, causing Wald confidence intervals to undercover asymptotically. Under regularity conditions, pathwise differentiability is restored if the uniformly bounded solution is unique at $P_0$. It is also restored, regardless of uniqueness, under the stronger requirement that the corresponding solution satisfy a uniformly bounded $\beta$-source condition for some $\beta$>0. We relate these regimes to very weak, weak, and strong identification in instrumental variables models.

entry.title: On the Optimisation Landscape of Overparameterised Weighted MMD

link.title: On the Optimisation Landscape of Overparameterised Weighted MMD

entry.content:
We study the optimisation landscape of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) over weighted atomic measures. For the one-dimensional Gaussian kernel, we show that, for any compactly supported target distribution, sufficiently many particles ensure that every local minimum has arbitrarily small MMD. Moreover, any stationary point whose MMD remains bounded away from zero is unstable under an unweighted gradient flow over the particle locations. These results hold both when the weights are constrained to the simplex, and when they are unconstrained but optimised at each step. When the target is itself finitely supported, we further strengthen this result: beyond an explicit particle threshold, there are no spurious local minima, and every spurious stationary point is unstable. To our knowledge, these are the first finite-particle overparameterisation guarantees of their kind for weighted MMD optimisation.

entry.title: Optimizing Sparse Boolean Rule Networks using Mixed Integer Linear Programming

link.title: Optimizing Sparse Boolean Rule Networks using Mixed Integer Linear Programming

entry.content:
We study the problem of learning accurate and cognitively simple binary classifiers that are directly interpretable as Boolean rules. We propose mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulations for training sparse disjunctive normal form (DNF) networks, viewed as small networks with a conjunctive hidden layer and a disjunctive output layer. Contrary to previous work that uses MILP for inductive rule learning, we start with a fixed network structure, for which we then find optimal weights. A regularized objective explicitly trades off misclassification costs against sparsity, yielding globally optimized rule sets. Our main technical contribution is an enhanced formulation that substantially reduces the number of integer decision variables and eliminates redundant constraints, while preserving exact Boolean semantics for all feasible solutions. Furthermore, we develop a combined approach based on initialization and dropout to break symmetries in the weights between rules, mitigating redundancy, and encouraging more diverse and stable rule representations. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and UCI datasets show that the advanced formulation improves computational efficiency and achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to established interpretable baselines, including SAT-based DNF learning and well-known rule- and tree-based learners. entry.title: Outperforming 1000 Euclidean Layers With Hyperbolic Goal-Conditioned RL

link.title: Outperforming 1000 Euclidean Layers With Hyperbolic Goal-Conditioned RL

entry.content:
Scaling self-supervised contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) to 1000-layer Euclidean neural networks has enabled state-of-the-art goal-reaching performance, yet wall-clock time scales linearly with depth. We find that changing the geometry achieves stronger performance with far shallower networks. This matters in complex navigation environments, where walls can make route distance deviate substantially from Euclidean distance. In a U-shaped maze, we show that the longer the route, the more it deviates from Euclidean distance. Hyperbolic CRL addresses this mismatch by replacing Euclidean distances in CRL’s contrastive objective with geodesic distances in hyperbolic space. On hard navigation tasks, inductive bias beats scale: depth 64 hyperbolic agents outperform 1024-layer-deep Euclidean networks while training more than $12 \times$ faster and using about $13 \times$ fewer parameters. We observe that hyperbolic agents behave qualitatively better in hard humanoid mazes, where they follow corridors to reach goals, whereas Euclidean agents try straight-line shortcuts over walls. Our results show that matching the representation geometry to the task can substitute for substantial network depth. Code is at https://github.com/Probabilistic-and-Interactive-ML/HypGCRL .

entry.title: Posterior Frequencies and the Cost of Not Fitting: A Correction to a Memorization Lower Bound

link.title: Posterior Frequencies and the Cost of Not Fitting: A Correction to a Memorization Lower Bound

entry.content:
Feldman’s memorization lower bound assigns a frequency coefficient based on how often a point appears in the training sample. We give an exact three-point counterexample to its conditional and averaged forms, using independent fair labels and a permutation-equivariant learner. A sequence of sampling priors makes the ratio of the proposed penalty to actual excess risk grow exponentially, ruling out a universal positive constant-factor repair. The priors vary with sample size, the offending profiles become rare, and both quantities vanish. Retaining the original model, we obtain an exact replacement using full-sample posterior probabilities. Under exchangeability, these depend on multiplicity and the complete frequency profile. We characterize the largest multiplicity-only coefficients valid for unrestricted learners. The original coefficient has the posterior-mean form of Good’s exact frequency formula and is an occupancy-weighted average of the corrected coefficients.

entry.title: Predicting future insurance markets: Simulation of technology adoption paths with a Bayesian Bass model

link.title: Predicting future insurance markets: Simulation of technology adoption paths with a Bayesian Bass model

entry.content:
Technological progress can give rise to new loss exposures or reduce existing risks. In either case, it strongly affects insurance companies’ existing lines of business. As the magnitude of such effects is often closely connected to the innovation’s market penetration, reliably predicting its adoption process is vital in enabling insurers to adapt their business strategy accordingly. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel combination of contributions from the domain of innovation diffusion. Our methodology generates adoption scenarios that holistically account for different sources of uncertainty, offers a structured way to incorporate expert judgment and insights from pre-existing technologies, and updates its predictions as new information on the technology’s diffusion becomes available. Its modular nature ensures that components can be easily replaced by suitable alternatives. Using publicly accessible data on privately-owned battery electric vehicles in Germany, the application of our approach for predicting changes to insurance losses and for supporting insurers’ sustainability strategies is visualized in a motor insurance case study.

entry.title: Predictively Oriented Gaussian Process Posteriors

link.title: Predictively Oriented Gaussian Process Posteriors

entry.content:
Gaussian Processes (GPs) are a powerful tool for modelling and quantifying uncertainty in functional relationships. However, they require practitioners to make a number of design decisions, such as the choice of the kernel and the observation model. Suboptimal choices can produce misspecified models that do not capture the underlying data generating process. We introduce Predictively Oriented Gaussian Processes (PrO-GPs), which treat predictive uncertainty as the primary inferential target and provide a robust alternative to standard GPs. Although direct computation of a PrO posterior for nonparametric models is intractable, we derive a reduced formulation and practical sampling scheme for efficient computation. Through synthetic and real data experiments, we show that PrO-GPs produce better calibrated predictive distributions under model misspecification compared to standard GP approaches.

entry.title: Principal Component Analysis for Zero-Inflated Probability Measures via Lorenz Curves

link.title: Principal Component Analysis for Zero-Inflated Probability Measures via Lorenz Curves

entry.content:
This paper develops a principal component analysis framework for probability measures associated with non-negative real-valued random variables with structural zeros. Specifically, leveraging the associated Lorenz Curve (LC) and a suitable perspective transformation of the plane, a bijective embedding is defined to treat such measures as functional data in a Hilbert space. Once the random LC is embedded in this space, standard Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) becomes directly applicable, and the diffeomorphic nature of the embedding allows the main convergence results and their interpretations to be transferred back to the original space of LC. The a.s. and $L^2(\mathbb{P})$ consistency of the estimated eigenfunctions, eigenvalues, and modes of variation is subsequently investigated, both in the embedded space and, by virtue of the embedding’s diffeomorphism property, in the original LC space. Crucially, this consistency analysis accounts for the double stochasticity of the estimation problem: one level of randomness is tied to the underlying LC process itself, while the other stems from the empirical estimation of the LC from sample data. As a consequence, consistency of the Karhunen–Lo`eve reconstructions is also established, guaranteeing faithful approximation of individual curves in both spaces. Finally, the proposed FPCA methodology is illustrated on a real-world dataset of global export flows and compared with a naive FPCA approach.

entry.title: Principal stratification with continuous treatments and continuous post-treatment variables

link.title: Principal stratification with continuous treatments and continuous post-treatment variables

entry.content:
Principal stratification (PS) is a commonly used approach for understanding the mechanisms through which a treatment affects an outcome. The goal of this work is to extend the PS framework to studies with continuous treatments, which introduces a number of both challenges and opportunities in terms of defining causal effects and performing inference. This manuscript provides multiple key methodological contributions: 1) we introduce principal causal estimands for continuous treatments that provide insights into different causal mechanisms, 2) we show that nonparametric identification is possible under a principal ignorability assumption, but only under a restrictive assumption on the joint distribution of potential mediators, which can be dropped under certain parametric assumptions, 3) we utilize nonparametric Bayesian models for the joint distribution of the potential mediating variables to mitigate issues from model misspecification, and 4) we provide theoretical justification for utilizing an outcome model to identify the joint distribution of the potential mediating variables, and show that this is only possible if a principal ignorability assumption is violated. Lastly, we illustrate our methodology by applying it to a novel study of the relationship between the economy and arrest rates, and how this is potentially mediated by police capacity.

entry.title: Principled Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization

link.title: Principled Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization

entry.content:
Expected improvement based on stochastic kriging (SK) surrogate is widely used in continuous simulation optimization, but unknown heteroscedastic noise makes three basic design choices consequential: the incumbent to define improvement, replication allocation, and final recommendation. Existing methods typically either assume the noise levels are known or choose these components separately through heuristic rules or empirical calibration. We instead derive a high-probability upper bound on the simple regret and systematically choose the three components within general rule classes to tighten this bound. We first establish a finite-sample confidence bound for the SK predictor as a foundation for the three design choices. Within general posterior-quantile rule classes, tightening the regret certificate selects a lower-quantile incumbent and an upper-quantile recommendation among sampled designs. The opposing quantiles reflect the different roles of exploratory experiments and the final implemented decision. Under mild conditions satisfied by common kernels, minimizing a tractable kernel-specific bound yields a logarithmic replication order. Based on these design choices, the resulting simple regret matches the existing results under known homoscedastic noise up to logarithmic factors. To our knowledge, this is the first simple-regret guarantee of this form for a continuous-domain EI-type simulation optimization method that learns unknown heteroscedastic variances through replications.

entry.title: Probabilistic AI models outperform numerical weather prediction models on record breaking heat extremes

link.title: Probabilistic AI models outperform numerical weather prediction models on record breaking heat extremes

entry.content:
AI weather prediction (AIWP) models have emerged as a key complement to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, and now often outperform them on aggregate skill. Yet, several studies report that physics-based models still forecast extreme events better, in particular record-breaking extremes, based on the evaluation of deterministic forecasts. Here we evaluate heat extreme forecasts from probabilistic AIWP models over global land and show that they clearly outperform the ECMWF IFS ensemble, both raw and post-processed, including for record-breaking events, in all regions and at all lead times considered. AIWP models better forecast the occurrence and intensity of extremes, are better calibrated in the tail and miss fewer records. Station observations confirm these results. We argue that many reported AIWP limitations stem from unsuitable verification choices, specifically comparing deterministic forecasts that target different quantities. Instead, a fair evaluation of extremes necessitates probabilistic verification.

entry.title: Projected Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Flows for Hawkes Background-Intensity Estimation

link.title: Projected Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Flows for Hawkes Background-Intensity Estimation

entry.content:
We consider the problem of estimating the background intensity of a Hawkes process when the triggering mechanism is known, treating the background as an unknown finite positive measure with a regular density. We propose a likelihood-based variational approach based on the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao geometry. In this setting, the relevant first variations are naturally distribution-valued and therefore fall outside the classical gradient-flow formulation. We develop a distributional framework for the resulting dynamics and give them a finite-dimensional meaning through projections onto statistical manifolds. We identify the true background as the unique zero of a limiting generalized gradient and, under suitable stability, compactness, integrability and approximation conditions, establish a conditional consistency theorem for measurable estimators satisfying the empirical projected equations on events whose probabilities tend to one. Finally, we specialize the construction to Gaussian-mixture manifolds and obtain an explicit finite-dimensional scheme.

entry.title: Propensity score with factor loadings: evaluating the effect of the Paris Agreement on the returns of European stocks

link.title: Propensity score with factor loadings: evaluating the effect of the Paris Agreement on the returns of European stocks

entry.content:
Factor models for longitudinal data, where policy adoption is unconfounded with respect to a low-dimensional set of latent factor loadings, have become increasingly popular for causal inference. Most existing approaches, however, rely on a causal finite-sample approach or computationally intensive methods, limiting their applicability and external validity. In this paper, we propose a novel method for panel causal inference within a super-population framework, based on inverse propensity score weighting, where the propensity score is a function of latent factor loadings. The approach relaxes the traditional restrictive assumptions of causal panel methods, while offering advantages in terms of causal interpretability, policy relevance, and computational efficiency. Under standard assumptions, we develop a three-step estimation procedure for the ATT and derive its large-sample properties using M-estimation theory. Simulation results show that the proposed estimator remains reliable across a variety of designs, including settings with misspecified factor structure and weakly dependent errors. We apply the method to assess the causal effect of the Paris Agreement - a policy aimed at fostering the transition to a low-carbon economy - on European stock returns. Our empirical results suggest a statistically significant and negative short-run effect on the stock returns of firms that demonstrate a strong commitment to sustainability.

entry.title: ProximalFM: Amortized Proximal Causal Inference under Hidden Confounding

link.title: ProximalFM: Amortized Proximal Causal Inference under Hidden Confounding

entry.content:
Standard causal identification methods often assume no unmeasured confounding and can fail when relevant confounders are unobserved. Proximal causal inference instead uses proxy variables to identify effects under hidden confounding. However, nonparametric proximal estimation can be challenging in practice: recovering causal estimands such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) requires solving an ill-posed integral equation that is data-hungry, hyperparameter-sensitive, and optimization-unstable. Bayesian inference for such models provides a desirable alternative, mitigating these difficulties by regularizing through the prior. However, computing a posterior is itself challenging, as a typical likelihood function will include latent variables. Following the recent success of tabular foundation models in backdoor, instrumental variable, and frontdoor settings, we propose that prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are uniquely suited to resolve this bottleneck. Indeed, by training on synthetic data sampled from compliant structural causal models with access to oracle counterfactuals, we simplify the task substantially, amortizing the implied Bayesian operator inversion into a single transformer forward pass. Compared to prior literature that focuses primarily on point estimation, our model, ProximalFM, explicitly targets the Bayesian posterior distribution of the CATE. One unique aspect of this problem is that we need to provide Monte Carlo estimates of the oracle CATEs, leading to a novel variation of PFNs that accounts for the added stochastic error. Across a diverse suite of proximal regimes, ProximalFM achieves consistently strong CATE-estimation performance without dataset-specific tuning, with its largest advantage when latent confounding is substantial and the proxies are weakly informative; it also provides fast inference through a single amortized forward pass.

entry.title: Q-Edge: Symmetry-Reduced Quantum Simulation of Structured Extreme Dependence

link.title: Q-Edge: Symmetry-Reduced Quantum Simulation of Structured Extreme Dependence

entry.content:
High-dimensional simulation of multivariate extremes is fundamentally limited by the combinatorial complexity of dependence, often more than by the scarcity of extreme observations. We show that symmetry admits a lossless orbit-space representation that preserves structured extreme dependence while replacing an exponentially large dependence space with a compact set of symmetry classes. Based on this principle, we develop Q-Edge (Quantum Extreme Dependence Engine), a symmetry-reduced quantum framework that operates directly in orbit space, enabling scalable simulation and digital twins of structured extreme systems. By transferring symmetry into the data representation rather than the quantum circuit, Q-Edge allows unconstrained quantum generative models to exploit dramatically reduced state spaces. For a 30-dimensional problem, approximately 1.6 million angular states collapse to 256 orbit states, reducing the required quantum representation from about 21 qubits to 8. Our results establish a general computational principle for scalable quantum simulation of structured extreme dependence.

link.title: Relative Bias Under Imperfect Identification in Observational Causal Inference

entry.content:
To conduct causal inference in observational settings, researchers must rely on certain identifying assumptions. In practice, these assumptions are unlikely to hold exactly. This paper considers the bias of selection-on-observables, instrumental variables, and proximal inference estimates under violations of their identifying assumptions. We develop bias expressions for IV and proximal inference that show how violations of their respective assumptions are amplified by any unmeasured confounding in the outcome variable. We propose a set of sensitivity tools that quantify the sensitivity of different identification strategies, and an augmented bias contour plot visualizes the relationship between these strategies. We argue that the act of choosing an identification strategy implicitly expresses a belief about the degree of violations that must be present in alternative identification strategies. Even when researchers intend to conduct an IV or proximal analysis, a sensitivity analysis comparing different identification strategies can help to better understand the implications of each set of assumptions. Throughout, we compare the different approaches on a re-analysis of the impact of state surveillance on the incidence of protest in Communist Poland.

entry.title: Relatively Smart II: Tractable or Semi-Supervised Instance-Optimal Learning

link.title: Relatively Smart II: Tractable or Semi-Supervised Instance-Optimal Learning

entry.content:
We continue the study of relatively smart learning, introduced by Dughmi and Pour (2026), which asks a supervised learner to compete, marginal by marginal, with every distribution-fixed error guarantee soundly certifiable from unlabeled data. They showed that the One-Inclusion Graph (OIG) learner is relatively smart with a quadratic sample-complexity blowup, and that no relatively smart learner can do better, leaving open whether ERM or another natural or tractable learner achieves comparable guarantees. They also left open whether the blowup can be restricted to unlabeled data. Our firs results shows that ERM—and in fact any proper consistent learner—is relatively smart for binary classification in the distribution-free setting. We show that a small certifiable error with $m$ samples implies a similarly small error on the uniform distribution over a random sample of size $O(m^2)$, yielding a cover of size at most $2^{m+1}$ on that sample. This suffices to control the error of proper consistent learners with $O(m^2)$ samples. We then show that semi-supervised relatively smart learning is information-theoretically possible with a quadratic blowup only in unlabeled sample complexity and no blowup in labeled sample complexity. The learner uses a natural generalization of OIG to a leave-most-out transductive problem, where labels of part of a finite pool are revealed and the remaining labels are predicted. Finally, this label efficiency comes at a cost in simplicity and tractability. If the hypothesis class is accessed only through an agnostic ERM oracle, any semi-supervised relatively smart learner with substantially sub-quadratic labeled-sample blowup requires super-polynomially many oracle calls. This holds even when the marginal is given explicitly, and thus also yields an intractability result for distribution-fixed learning that may be of independent interest.

entry.title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials

link.title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials

entry.content:
Automated materials discovery requires evaluating large pools of candidate configurations, with density functional theory (DFT) as a major throughput bottleneck. Pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate DFT cheaply, but their errors vary by orders of magnitude across configurations, making it difficult to decide when to trust the MLIP predictions and when to fall back to DFT. We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $\alpha$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $\alpha=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP’s latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

entry.title: Robust inference for risk heterogeneity under group imbalance

link.title: Robust inference for risk heterogeneity under group imbalance

entry.content:
Population-level heterogeneity is ubiquitous in biomedical data, where differences across demographic or clinical subgroups can substantially alter risk patterns. For example, in intensive care unit (ICU) studies, the mortality risk associated with specific admission diagnoses can vary across ethnic groups. Existing approaches for detecting risk heterogeneity are often sensitive to baseline model misspecification and regularization bias, both of which commonly arise in practice. In this paper, we propose a robust framework for inferring risk heterogeneity between two populations using Neyman orthogonality, which yields estimators that are locally insensitive to nuisance parameter estimation error. The proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and simulation studies demonstrate that in finite samples our method substantially reduces bias and improves inferential stability compared with standard likelihood-based approaches. In an application to the eICU Collaborative Research Database, our method reveals clinically meaningful ethnicity-specific heterogeneity in admission diagnoses for in-hospital mortality that standard likelihood-based methods fail to detect.

entry.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation

link.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation

entry.content:
We introduce SNACK, a string representation for probabilistic graph generation that enables sequence models to generate and model graphs with discrete node and edge features. SNACK linearizes graphs by encoding the nonzero entries of the lower-triangular adjacency matrix, establishing a bijective correspondence between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices. This design enables invalid logit masking to enforce structural constraints–such as chemical valence and ordering rules–guaranteeing 100% valid generated sequences. SNACK also enables principled string-based GFlowNet training by explicitly accounting for node-ordering symmetries. Across standard graph-generation tasks and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks, SNACK achieves competitive sample quality, while substantially improving the throughput of GFlowNet training relative to graph-based generation. Probing analyses further show that models trained on SNACK encode meaningful local and global graph structure despite receiving only sequential supervision. These results position SNACK as a practical framework for probabilistic graph generation with deep sequence models.

entry.title: SULA: Robust Langevin Sampling via Drift-Diffusion Saturation

link.title: SULA: Robust Langevin Sampling via Drift-Diffusion Saturation

entry.content:
The unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and its stochastic-gradient variant, SGLD, are workhorses of modern Bayesian machine learning, but can be fragile when faced with a target distribution possessing a non-Lipschitz drift. In such settings, the expected squared jump distance can grow rapidly, leading to numerical instability or the need for prohibitively small step-sizes. We propose the saturated unadjusted Langevin algorithm (SULA) that pairs a saturated gradient drift with a gradient-informed state-dependent diffusion, while preserving first-order consistency with the Langevin diffusion. The drift and diffusion terms are chosen to guarantee that the one-step squared update is independent of the gradient. Consequently, SULA is robust to the choice of step-size and preserves estimation and prediction quality. We provide sufficient conditions under which SULA with a step-size $h$ converges weakly to the Langevin diffusion at the standard $O(h)$ rate, the SULA chain is geometrically ergodic, and that the bias of its invariant measure relative to the target is $O(h)$. Further, we develop SG-SULA, a stochastic-gradient version of SULA that rescales the stochastic gradient using a Gaussian CDF correction under Gaussianity of the gradient noise. Numerical experiments on various examples demonstrate SULA’s robustness to tuning and SG-SULA’s improved predictive performance.

entry.title: Self-Organized Conformal Prediction: Reducing Regional Coverage Gaps with Unsupervised Group Discovery

link.title: Self-Organized Conformal Prediction: Reducing Regional Coverage Gaps with Unsupervised Group Discovery

entry.content:
Conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage, but a pooled calibration quantile can hide systematic undercoverage across heterogeneous regions of the feature space. We introduce Self-Organized Conformal Prediction (SOCP), a calibration scheme that discovers input-space groups with an unsupervised Self-Organizing Map (SOM) trained without calibration data. At prediction time, the query’s best-matching unit (BMU) retrieves a calibration buffer from one cell, a fixed grid neighborhood, or a prototype enlargement (Regimes 1 to 3). When fixed neighborhoods are too sparse, Regime 3 adds cells by prototype distance, using a global budget selected from training cell occupancies and the planned calibration size before any calibration score is observed. The predictor and nonconformity score remain unchanged. Cell-only retrieval has exact cell-conditional validity, and each fixed union of cells has exact retrieved-set validity. Interpreting a neighborhood threshold at its central cell incurs an explicit Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) bias term. Across ten regression and classification benchmarks, SOCP lowers the mean weighted coverage gap (WCovGap) relative to pooled split conformal prediction (SCP) on all ten datasets. The mean relative change is -14.8%, with a mean increase of 3.0% in output size. Under fixed-neighborhood retrieval, SO calibration lowers mean WCovGap across ten seeds in 43 of 50 score and dataset comparisons, while SO-SCP lowers it for every dataset at all three tested external partition granularities. These results provide local group calibration without supervised partitions or predictor retraining, while the diagnostics make the cost and limits of locality explicit. The code is available at https://github.com/LouisTier/SOCP.

entry.title: Semi-Amortized Bayesian Inference with Reusable Local Posteriors

link.title: Semi-Amortized Bayesian Inference with Reusable Local Posteriors

entry.content:
Amortized Bayesian inference uses simulations to perform Bayesian estimation when likelihoods are expensive or analytically unavailable. However, learning the full joint posterior is challenging in high-dimensional models with complex dependencies. We introduce a semi-amortized method that divides parameters into smaller blocks, and uses conditional independence to identify the information needed to infer each block. We train neural estimators for blocks whose posterior updates are computationally expensive or frequently repeated. Each estimator learns from simulations of the relevant model components to approximate the block’s full conditional posterior, given the relevant observations and the values of the variables on which it depends. A Markov chain then alternates direct draws from these estimators with conventional updates of the remaining variables. Each neural update uses the current conditioning values and requires neither likelihood evaluation nor an acceptance-rejection step. Where the same conditional structure recurs, one estimator can be reused across blocks and datasets, with an output dimension determined by the block rather than the full model. We illustrate the approach in high-dimensional and computationally expensive hierarchical and spatiotemporal models.

entry.title: Sharp Statistical Thresholds for Attributed Gaussian Graph Matching

link.title: Sharp Statistical Thresholds for Attributed Gaussian Graph Matching

entry.content:
We investigate the problem of matching networks where both edge weights and node features are correlated following a specific node correspondence. While prior work has established sharp thresholds for matching either graphs or features individually, the joint setting has been significantly less explored. In this study, we derive precise information-theoretic thresholds for exact recovery, almost-exact recovery, and partial recovery of the underlying alignment. These are expressed in terms of graph and feature correlation strengths, the number of nodes, and the dimension of the features. Interestingly, whereas an all-or-nothing phase transition is observed in the standard graph-matching scenario, the inclusion of contextual information at the node level introduces a richer structure: the exact-recovery threshold separates from the shared threshold for almost-exact and partial recovery. Closing gaps left by prior works, we provide a sharp characterization of the thresholds governing how structural and contextual information interact in graph matching, and thereby establish a benchmark for designing efficient algorithms in the high-dimensional setting.

link.title: Shortest fixed-width confidence intervals for a bounded parameter: The Push algorithm

entry.content:
We present a method for computing optimal fixed-width confidence intervals for a single, bounded parameter, extending a method for the binomial due to Asparaouhov and Lorden, who called it the Push algorithm. The method produces the shortest possible non-decreasing confidence interval for a given confidence level, and if the Push interval does not exist for a given width and level, then no such interval exists. The method applies to any bounded parameter that is discrete, or is continuous for which interval probabilities are quasiconcave. We demonstrate the method on the binomial, hypergeometric, and normal distributions with our available R package. In each of these distributions the proposed method outperforms the standard ones, and in the latter case even improves upon the $z$-interval. We apply the proposed method to World Health Organization (WHO) data on tobacco use.

entry.title: Sig-DEG for Distillation: Making Diffusion Models Faster and Lighter

link.title: Sig-DEG for Distillation: Making Diffusion Models Faster and Lighter

entry.content:
Diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art generative performance but remain computationally expensive at inference, often requiring many discretization steps. We propose Sig-DEG (Signature-based Differential Equation Generator), a generator for distilling pre-trained diffusion models. Inspired by high-order stochastic Taylor expansions, Sig-DEG combines partial signatures that summarize Brownian motion over subintervals with a recurrent structure to approximate stochastic differential equation solutions to achieve universality. We formulate distillation as supervised learning, matching fine-resolution teacher trajectories on a coarse time grid. At inference, Sig-DEG enables fast generation, as the partial signatures can be simulated exactly from their known distributions without requiring fine-grained Brownian paths. Experiments on image and time-series generation demonstrate competitive sample quality with inference speedups of up to several hundred times over the teacher. A Schr"odinger bridge example further demonstrates Sig-DEG’s applicability beyond diffusion distillation.
