entry.title: Sign-Flipping Score Tests for Fixed Effects in Multivariate Clustered Data

link.title: Sign-Flipping Score Tests for Fixed Effects in Multivariate Clustered Data

entry.content:
Standard parametric inference on fixed effects in multivariate linear mixed models can be sensitive to covariance misspecification, particularly with multivariate responses. We propose clip, a clusterwise conditional resampling procedure based on effective scores and transformation-specific standardization. The procedure may use a working covariance to improve efficiency, but its validity does not require correct specification. When covariance parameters are estimated, they are estimated only once and held fixed across transformations. Together with synchronous transformations that avoid modeling between-response covariance, this facilitates joint inference for high-dimensional multivariate responses. Under a correctly specified marginal mean and suitable regularity conditions, we establish asymptotic validity for independent, heterogeneous clusters and derive a quantitative bound relating approximation accuracy to the magnitude and heterogeneity of clusterwise score contributions. Simulations show reliable type I error control and competitive power. An electroencephalography application illustrates simultaneous inference across correlated outcomes.

entry.title: Simulation Based Inference of a Simple Neural Network Structure

link.title: Simulation Based Inference of a Simple Neural Network Structure

entry.content:
Neurophysiologists are nowadays able to record from a large number of extracellular electrodes and to extract, from the raw data, the sequences of action potentials or spikes generated by many neurons. Unfortunately these ‘‘many neurons’’ still represent only a tiny fraction of the neuronal population that constitutes the network. Using association statistics such as the estimation of the cross-correlation functions, they are trying to infer the structure of the network formed by the recorded neurons. But this inference is compromised by the tremendous under-sampling of the neuronal population. We propose to focus instead on simple spike train statistics, like the empirical spikes frequency, or the interspike interval distribution. Their sampling distributions can be estimated by simulations, and, given a few observed spike train statistics, they provide enough information to infer the structure of the underlying network. We show that, on a ‘‘toy model’’, our method gives significantly better results than the sub-network reconstruction method with regards to the inference of the connection probability of the original network.

entry.title: SpectrumQuant: Spectrum Alignment for LLM Quantization

link.title: SpectrumQuant: Spectrum Alignment for LLM Quantization

entry.content:
Orthogonal transforms have emerged as an effective tool for low-bit quantization of large language models (LLMs), as they reshape activation distributions without changing the underlying model function. Existing approaches typically rely either on fixed data-agnostic transforms, such as Hadamard rotations, or on calibration-time optimization of learned rotations. We study rotation selection from first principles and show that maximizing covariance leads to spectral alignment and provides a principled criterion for constructing quantization-friendly orthogonal transforms. Based on this insight, we propose SpectrumQuant, a closed-form rotation method that estimates activation covariance from calibration data and uses it to construct a covariance-aware orthogonal transform for post-training quantization. Our formulation characterizes quantization-friendly rotations as compositions of alignment and mixing components, while recovering Hadamard matrices as a special case. Interestingly, a class of butterfly matrices belongs to this category. In the realm of LLM quantization, SpectrumQuant bridges the gap between data-agnostic structured rotations and learned rotations, providing an effective and efficient data-aware alternative for post-training quantization. Experiments on Llama and Mistral models show that SpectrumQuant is competitive with state-of-the-art rotation strategies while requiring less than one-third of the GPU memory and significantly less time than learned rotations approaches like SpinQuant and DartQuant.

entry.title: State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction

link.title: State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction

entry.content:
Sequential conformal prediction needs to decide which past errors should calibrate uncertainty for the current target. Recency and online error feedback are useful when recent observations remain relevant, but the recent past can be a poor reference when comparable states recur at nonadjacent times, with the recurrence pattern generally unknown. We propose State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction (SMSCP), which constructs an explicit one-sided local-linear state from pre-target information, uses state similarity to select a matched reference set of past calibration scores, and then applies the ordinary unweighted conformal order statistic. In contrast to existing approaches, SMSCP uses state similarity to identify calibration observations relevant to the target score quantile. This motivates a theoretical analysis of whether nearby states have comparable target score quantiles under temporal dependence. We establish control of the resulting conformal cutoff and characterize predictive information not captured by the chosen state. Simulations show that state matching is most effective when score-relevant states recur across nonadjacent times, while revealing settings in which its advantage weakens or reverses. Across solar irradiance and bike-demand benchmarks, SMSCP improves interval score over recency, weighted, adaptive, and HopCPT comparators, and achieves coverage closer to the nominal 0.90 level than ResCP on five of six benchmarks.

link.title: Steering Diffusion Models to Rare Events with Sequential Monte Carlo

entry.content:
Diffusion models are increasingly used as surrogates for expensive simulators in weather prediction, molecular dynamics, and materials design. In these models, computing the probability $p_0[E]$ of an event $E$ is difficult, especially when the event of interest is rare. A stable estimate using Monte Carlo becomes computationally intractable, requiring a growing sample size $\propto!1/p_0[E]$ to compensate for an increasing rarity. In this paper, we present Diffusion rare event sampling with Sequential Monte Carlo (DireSMC), a sequential Monte Carlo scheme that guides a population of weighted samples towards the rare event, giving access not only to samples but also to a calibrated estimate of its probability. We set up our guidance using an analytical relaxation of the event set, allowing the method to easily extend to a wide range of user-defined rare events. We validate our method on a toy problem with analytical solutions and on a score-based climate emulator, where we obtain accurate rare-event probabilities on a range of rarities from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-5}$, achieving net speed-ups of $9\times$ to $1413\times$ over Monte Carlo.

entry.title: Stereographic Multiple-Try Metropolis

link.title: Stereographic Multiple-Try Metropolis

entry.content:
Multiple-proposal MCMC algorithms have recently gained attention for their potential to improve performance, especially through parallel implementation on modern hardware. We introduce Stereographic Multiple-Try Metropolis (SMTM), a novel family of gradient-free algorithms designed for sampling high-dimensional distributions. By integrating multiple-try Metropolis (MTM) with the stereographic MCMC framework, SMTM overcomes the traditional limitations of MTM, particularly its pathological convergence behavior often observed in high dimensions. For both light-tailed and heavy-tailed targets, SMTM not only outperforms classical MTM and the existing stereographic random-walk Metropolis but also demonstrates strong robustness to tuning. These advantages are supported by high-dimensional scaling analysis and validated through extensive simulation studies.

entry.title: Strong Gaussian Approximation of Constant Learning Rate SGD: Bias and Trajectory Inference

link.title: Strong Gaussian Approximation of Constant Learning Rate SGD: Bias and Trajectory Inference

entry.content:
This paper develops strong Gaussian approximations (KMT type) for constant learning rate stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We work with heavy tailed noise and assume that the number of iterates grows and the learning rate shrinks simultaneously. Our work constructs simple Gaussian processes on the same space and bounds, in probability, the maximum difference between the SGD errors and their respective limits. While there exist central limit theorems for constant rate SGD centered at the optimum, these only provide individual iterate inference. By contrast, our quenched KMT approximations allow for finite sample, simultaneous, whole-trajectory-level inference and imply stochastic process convergence (Functional Central Limit Theorems (FCLTs)). For accumulated errors centered at the true optimum, we first obtain a KMT-type approximation bound when the learning rate scales as $\gamma_n=\frac{c}{\sqrt n}+o(n^{-1/2})$ for a constant $c \in \mathbb{R}^+$ and $n$ iterations. The result reveals a trade off between controlling the bias of SGD and the initialization effect, with no learning rate scaling generally making both contributions vanish in the accumulated error limit. To eliminate these contributions, we consider a Burn in scheme and Richardson-Romberg extrapolation and prove respective KMT and FCLT theorems. We also prove a finite-horizon KMT-type approximation and FCLT for the rescaled iterate trajectory to a stationary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process. We consider applications in risk control and simultaneous inference and perform simulations to illustrate our results.

entry.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent

link.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent

entry.content:
Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.

entry.title: Student Copula Markov Networks

link.title: Student Copula Markov Networks

entry.content:
This paper extends the applicability of probabilistic graphical models to non Gaussian data. It establishes a characterization of the pairwise Markov property in undirected probabilistic graphical models in terms of copula densities. Building on this characterization, we derive a necessary condition for the pairwise Markov property in Student copula Markov networks. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm (ECM) is provided to facilitate the penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies, which demonstrate its effectiveness in estimating model parameters and recovering the underlying graph structure.

entry.title: Subdata Selection for Measurement-Constrained Linear Regression under Model Misspecification

link.title: Subdata Selection for Measurement-Constrained Linear Regression under Model Misspecification

entry.content:
In many modern applications, obtaining response variables is costly, time-consuming, or technically challenging, making it impractical to measure outcomes for all available units. In such settings, covariates may be available for a large pool of candidates, but responses can only be collected for a small, carefully selected subset, making the choice of which units to measure a consequential decision. Most existing subsampling methods are developed for massive datasets, emphasizing the trade-off between statistical accuracy and computational cost, and typically relying on the assumption of a correctly specified model. These features limit their suitability in measurement-constrained settings, where statistical efficiency is paramount and model misspecification is often unavoidable. To address these challenges, we develop a new subset selection framework for linear regression that accommodates potential model misspecification. The proposed approach targets predictive expected loss and yields an A-optimality-type criterion that depends only on covariate information, requiring no response observations at the selection stage. We refer to this method as Expected Loss Optimal Selection (ELOS). By focusing on predictive risk rather than model-based optimality, ELOS remains well-defined and robust under misspecification. Simulation studies and real data applications demonstrate that ELOS achieves strong predictive performance and compares favorably with existing methods across a range of scenarios.

entry.title: Symmetry-Compatible Principle for Optimizer Design: Embeddings, LM Heads, SwiGLU MLPs, and MoE Routers

link.title: Symmetry-Compatible Principle for Optimizer Design: Embeddings, LM Heads, SwiGLU MLPs, and MoE Routers

entry.content:
A striking geometric disparity has long persisted in the practice of deep learning. While modern neural network architectures naturally exhibit rich symmetry and equivariance properties, popular optimizers such as Adam and its variants operate inherently coordinate-wise, rendering them unable to respect the equivariance structures of the parameter space. We address this disparity by introducing a symmetry-compatible principle for optimizer design: the gradient update rule should be equivariant under the symmetry group acting on the corresponding weight block. Following this principle, we first provide a unified perspective on bi-orthogonally equivariant updates for general matrix layers, as employed by stochastic spectral descent, Muon, Scion, and polar gradient methods. More importantly, by moving from orthogonal groups to permutation and shared-shift symmetries, we derive symmetry-compatible optimizers for parameter blocks whose symmetries differ from those of general matrix layers: embedding and LM head matrices, SwiGLU MLP projections, and MoE router matrices. These constructions include one-sided spectral, row-norm, hybrid row-norm/spectral, row-aware, column-aware, centered row-norm, and left-spectral updates. They yield an end-to-end layerwise optimizer stack in which each major matrix-valued parameter class is assigned an update whose equivariance matches its symmetry group. We corroborate this principle through pre-training experiments on dense and sparse MoE language models, including Qwen3-0.6B-style, Gemma 3 1B-style, OLMoE-1B-7B-style, and downsized gpt-oss architectures. Across these experiments, symmetry-compatible update rules consistently improve final validation loss, reduce expert load imbalance in sparse MoE models, and in several cases control final vocabulary-logit growth, improve router stability, and overall training stability over the corresponding AdamW updates.

entry.title: Target-Constrained Pooling for Trajectory Extrapolation

link.title: Target-Constrained Pooling for Trajectory Extrapolation

entry.content:
Trajectory extrapolation from a partial target trajectory is underdetermined, but completed related trajectories provide information about the unresolved continuation. We propose target-constrained pooling (TCP), which separates the finite-horizon endpoint from continuation shape and estimates that endpoint from two complementary source signals. Uniform pooling captures final response levels, while matched-increment pooling captures the remaining change after aligning source and target states. TCP selects representative sources, projects both endpoint estimates onto a target-consistent region, converts them into corrections of the free forecast, and controls their influence through strength calibration and degradation-aware weighting. Across 25,245 targets from five domains and both forecasting directions, TCP reduces mean RMSE by 35.8% to 42.1% for all ten target-only forecasters and improves all 100 forecaster, dataset, and direction comparisons. The two endpoint signals consistently outperform either alone, while representative selection remains within 0.64% to 1.02% of the full donor pool using 12.7x fewer donor inputs and 138.8x fewer matching distance computations.

entry.title: Testing Conditional Distribution Equality Using Generative Models

link.title: Testing Conditional Distribution Equality Using Generative Models

entry.content:
Conditional distribution equality testing is a core problem with applications in causal inference, model diagnostics, and transfer learning. Existing methods often lose power when the conditioning variable is high-dimensional. We propose a new test that leverages generative models to compare conditional distributions using both observed data and synthetic samples. A sample-splitting and studentization scheme is introduced to control estimation error. Under the null, the test statistic is asymptotically normal, and we establish local power against contiguous alternatives. Our theory under the null and fixed alternative requires only consistency of the learned conditional distribution, allowing for a broad class of generative models. Empirical results demonstrate accurate size control and strong power in high-dimensional settings compared to representative kernel-based conditional and joint two-sample tests.

entry.title: Testing Cumulative Treatment Effects in Continuous Time with ODE Dynamics and Noisy Observations

link.title: Testing Cumulative Treatment Effects in Continuous Time with ODE Dynamics and Noisy Observations

entry.content:
We develop a semiparametric continuous time inferential framework for testing cumulative treatment effects, including both immediate and carryover effects. The latent state process is modeled by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose drift depends on state and treatment, while the observed data are noisy measurements of this latent state at irregular, multi resolution time points. We define the average treatment effect (ATE) as the difference of expected cumulative outcomes under the always treat and always control policies and establish its identifiability from observational data. More generally, the framework accommodates contrasts between arbitrary deterministic stationary treatment policies, including clinically motivated threshold policies, with the always treat versus never treat comparison as the leading special case. A two step estimation procedure first recovers the latent state trajectories and their derivatives via spline smoothing, then solves a continuous time estimating equation derived from the infinitesimal generator of the ODE. We prove asymptotic normality of the resulting test statistic under explicit rate conditions on the spline estimator. The resulting test admits asymptotically valid inference under noisy, irregularly sampled observations, providing a studentized statistic with a standard $N(0,1)$ limit. Simulations show that the proposed method demonstrates improved stability and power over discrete time alternatives in noisy and multi resolution settings, with comparable performance under clean regular grids. We apply the method to the OhioT1DM diabetes dataset to evaluate cumulative effects of insulin treatments on glucose levels.

entry.title: Testing for Peer Effects in Heteroskedastic Fixed-Effects Panels

link.title: Testing for Peer Effects in Heteroskedastic Fixed-Effects Panels

entry.content:
We study testing for peer effects in linear panel models with individual and time fixed effects when the interaction network is unspecified. We propose a quadratic-form test based on the Gram matrix of residualized peer covariates. A key difficulty is that fixed-effects removal and nuisance estimation destroy the centering of a conventional leave-diagonal-out quadratic form under conditional heteroskedasticity. We introduce a leverage adjustment that restores exact conditional centering and combine it with a residual-based variance estimator. The resulting studentized statistic is asymptotically standard normal as both panel dimensions diverge, without imposing any restriction on their relative growth rates. Under additional conditions, we establish consistency against alternatives. The null theory is further extended to covariates that are weakly dependent over time; the same studentization remains valid without an additional long-run variance estimator. Monte Carlo experiments evaluate the finite-sample size and power of the proposed test across different settings and demonstrate its favorable performance relative to the existing benchmark test. Applications to state tax competition and growth spillovers among OECD countries illustrate the practical relevance in testing for peer effects without specifying the interaction network.

entry.title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance

link.title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance

entry.content:
In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.

entry.title: The Critical Line Algorithm and the Constrained LASSO: One Curve, Two Literatures

link.title: The Critical Line Algorithm and the Constrained LASSO: One Curve, Two Literatures

entry.content:
Many statistical procedures compute an entire solution path rather than a single estimator. For one class the path is piecewise linear, traced corner to corner by an active-set homotopy. Two of its members coincide exactly: under $\Sigma=X^\top X$ and $\mu=X^\top y$ the gross-exposure-constrained mean–variance program and the constrained LASSO trace the same piecewise-linear curve, and they keep doing so under arbitrary linear equality and inequality constraints. Which parameter is swept, a leverage budget or a return tilt, is not a choice the curve notices: under a homogeneous mandate the two sweeps differ by a scalar. A mandate that holds the portfolio invested costs a radial rescaling instead, and the efficient frontier is that curve rescaled; its corners pass unnoticed because the frontier is continuously differentiable where they fall. We give the map between the two parametrisations and the single way it degenerates. That mean–variance selection and the LASSO instantiate one parametric quadratic program is prior art (G"artner, Jaggi and Maria, 2012). The Critical Line Algorithm itself lies off that route, and the correspondence established here is new. The identity is one of curves, not of statistical experiments. The map between the parametrisations is computed from the data, so the geometry of the path transfers while quantities averaged over the response do not. We cross that boundary deliberately and give the degrees of freedom of the constrained fit under arbitrary linear constraints. In the long-only, fully invested case it is the expected number of holdings away from a bound, less one.

entry.title: The Efficient Frontier from a LASSO Solver

link.title: The Efficient Frontier from a LASSO Solver

entry.content:
Schmelzer and Hastie prove that Markowitz’s Critical Line Algorithm and the LASSO path trace the same curve. This companion note checks that result numerically with a stock LASSO solver, \texttt{lars_path} from \texttt{scikit-learn}, and no portfolio software. entry.title: The LR2 Lifetime Distribution: Rate Crossing, Reliability Properties, and Estimation

link.title: The LR2 Lifetime Distribution: Rate Crossing, Reliability Properties, and Estimation

entry.content:
We study the LR2 one-parameter lifetime distribution obtained by mixing an exponential component of rate $\theta/2$ and a gamma component with shape four and rate $\theta^2$. The exponential mixing probability is $\theta^2/(1+\theta^2)$ for $\theta>0$. We derive the density, survival function, moments, transforms, truncated moments, quantiles, order-statistic distributions, mean residual life, and stress–strength reliability. Identifiability follows from the density at the origin, and strict monotonicity of the mean yields a unique moment estimator. A complete density-turning-point criterion and analytic initial and tail hazard expansions clarify the possible shapes. The component rates cross at one half. The hazard decreases initially for every positive parameter and eventually increases in the gamma-dominated regime; it eventually decreases in the exponential-dominated regime. We develop likelihood estimation, observed information, constrained expectation–maximization, spacing estimation, and inference under regularity conditions, and state the likelihood for independent right censoring. A reproducible Monte Carlo study with eight settings and 4,000 generated samples compares likelihood and moment estimation and evaluates log-scale confidence intervals. The analysis distinguishes mathematical properties from empirical validation and explains the restrictions associated with a fixed working time unit.

entry.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation

link.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation

entry.content:
Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models’ training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

entry.title: The Statistical Benefits of Multiple Responses for Learning from Demonstrations

link.title: The Statistical Benefits of Multiple Responses for Learning from Demonstrations

entry.content:
Many generative systems return multiple candidate responses and are evaluated according to the best one. Recent work shows that, when demonstrations are optimal, pass@$k$ can reduce the sample complexity of learning from demonstrations by a logarithmic factor in $k$. We ask what happens when the demonstrator is not assumed to be optimal. We find that multiple responses provide a qualitatively stronger benefit in this setting. In a finite reward-class model with no reward feedback, moving from pass@$1$ to any pass@$k$ with $k\ge2$ changes the worst-case dependence on target accuracy from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$, uniformly over demonstrator quality. Under standard evaluation, where an unknown reward is fixed before training, increasing $k$ provides an additional and distinct benefit: the optimal dependence on a reward class of size $N$ improves from $\log N$ to $\log N/\log k$. We further show that these two effects can be separated. Under robust evaluation, where one learned policy must compete with the demonstrator simultaneously for every reward in the class, the fast $1/\varepsilon$ dependence persists, while the $1/\log k$ improvement can disappear. We establish matching upper and lower bounds in the corresponding regimes and give a greedy multiplicative-weights learner achieving the upper bounds without any assumption on demonstrator quality.

entry.title: The Zero Pattern of a Design Matrix Drives Multiple Descent in Over-parameterized Regression

link.title: The Zero Pattern of a Design Matrix Drives Multiple Descent in Over-parameterized Regression

entry.content:
Over-parameterized linear regression has been widely studied over the last decade. However, most existing works assume that the covariates are independent and that their covariance matrices are non-degenerate. In this paper, we relax both assumptions and derive deterministic equivalents for the prediction risk in a vanishing-ridge regime. We show that degeneracy of the covariance matrices and dependence can lead to multiple descent, and characterize where the corresponding peaks can occur. Our proofs use a novel graph representation of the variance profile. We show that maximum matchings and the Dulmage–Mendelsohn decomposition of the associated bipartite graph identify the configurations at which the variance becomes singular.

entry.title: The long shadow of pandemic: Understanding the lingering effects of cause-specific mortality shocks

link.title: The long shadow of pandemic: Understanding the lingering effects of cause-specific mortality shocks

entry.content:
In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, empirical data have revealed that large-scale health crises not only cause immediate disruptions in mortality dynamics but also have persistent effects that may last for several years. Existing mortality models largely assume that mortality shocks are transitory and overlook how their effects can be long-lasting and heterogeneous across age groups and causes of death. In response to this limitation, we propose a novel stochastic mortality model that captures age- and cause-specific long-lasting effects of mortality jumps through a gamma-density-like decay function, estimated via a customized conditional maximum likelihood algorithm. Applying the model to recent U.S. mortality data, we reveal divergent persistence patterns across demographic groups and provide key insights into the tail risk profiles of life insurance and annuity products. Our scenario-based analyses further show that neglecting persistent shock effects can lead to suboptimal hedging, while the proposed model enables what-if testing to analyze such effects under potential future health crises.

entry.title: The minimal width of neural networks and immersions of real projective space

link.title: The minimal width of neural networks and immersions of real projective space

entry.content:
We investigate the minimal width of deep neural networks that can approximate all continuous functions from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ in the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets. We show that whenever the real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$ admits a smooth immersion into $\mathbb{R}^n$, the minimal width is at least $n+\min{n,m}$, assuming that the activation function is continuous and monotone. As a consequence, the minimal width of ReLU networks is $n+m$ whenever $n$ is equal to 2, 3, 4, 7 or 8 and $1\le m \le n$, extending results of Hanin-Sellke and Hwang. This suggests an intriguing connection between the approximation theory of neural networks and differential topology.

entry.title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology

link.title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology

entry.content:
Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.

entry.title: Thompson Sampling for Learning in Zero-Sum Games

link.title: Thompson Sampling for Learning in Zero-Sum Games

entry.content:
Thompson sampling (TS) achieves logarithmic and asymptotically optimal regret in classical stochastic bandits, but its behavior in multi-agent learning remains less understood. We study TS in an unknown finite two-player zero-sum matrix game with Gaussian bandit feedback. Under centralized self-play, TS samples a single payoff matrix from the posterior and plays a Nash equilibrium of the sampled game. For every fixed zero-sum game with a unique Nash equilibrium, we show that the expected cumulative duality gap is $O(\sqrt T)$. The rate improves to $O(\log T)$ for pure equilibria. We then identify the exact coefficient of the $\sqrt T$ term, which depends only on the equilibrium strategies and the noise level. We also establish a minimax lower bound matching the square-root dependence on $T$ and an instance-dependent lower bound matching the logarithmic dependence on $T$ for a class of games with a unique pure equilibrium. Experiments support the predicted rates and coefficient.

entry.title: Tracking a Small Set of Experts in Online Convex Optimization

link.title: Tracking a Small Set of Experts in Online Convex Optimization

entry.content:
For the fundamental problem of prediction from expert advice, Freund asked whether one could compete with a comparator that switches $k$ times among only $m$ experts. For a discrete set of experts, this problem was resolved by Bousquet and Warmuth (2020), who gave an efficient algorithm with optimal regret matching the information-theoretic limit. We study the analogous problem in online convex optimization, where the action space is continuous. An inefficient algorithm can be derived by discretizing the action space and applying the Bousquet–Warmuth algorithm, giving regret of $\widetilde{O}(md+k)$, while the best known efficient algorithm for this problem has regret $\widetilde{O}(dk)$. We show that this computational inefficiency is inherent, establishing a separation between the information-theoretic and polynomial-time regret achievable for this problem. Specifically, under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, we show that for every polynomial-time algorithm there exist instances for which it incurs at least $(k\sqrt d)^{1-o(1)}$ regret.

entry.title: Two Gaussians, Too Many: A bootstrap-based approach to assess identifiability in non-Gaussian structural vector autoregressions

link.title: Two Gaussians, Too Many: A bootstrap-based approach to assess identifiability in non-Gaussian structural vector autoregressions

entry.content:
Normality pre-tests on reduced-form innovations cannot detect whether two or more underlying structural shocks are Gaussian, and hence cannot detect a failure of identification in non-Gaussian SVARs. We propose a bootstrap-based approach that reveals such a failure. Under the null of valid identification and certain regularity conditions, the conditional bootstrap distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator of the impact matrix is asymptotically normal, so the diagnostic reduces to a normality test on the bootstrap replications. The impact-matrix estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal when one shock is Gaussian and its shape parameter lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so the diagnostic is valid across the entire null hypothesis. When the number of bootstrap replications and the sample size diverge jointly at an appropriate rate, the test statistic, conditional on the data, is asymptotically pivotal. This implies that conditioning on this diagnostic does not induce pre-testing bias asymptotically. In simulations with Normal-inverse Gaussian shocks, the multivariate diagnostic is close to its nominal size under the null, its power against an additional Gaussian shock increases with the sample size, and its univariate version localizes the failure in large samples. Based on the estimates of a SVAR in the macroeconomic and financial uncertainty literature, we demonstrate its potential as a practical, robust tool for assessing non-Gaussian identification.

link.title: Vine Copula VAR:From Recursive Margins to Joint Forecast Inference

entry.content:
Joint-event forecasts combine an estimated dependence model with current marginal forecasts. Retaining historical transforms at the marginal fits available when each outcome arrived creates overlapping estimation errors. We derive their joint influence with the terminal estimates in a stable Vine Copula VAR with normal innovation margins and a fixed, correctly specified Gaussian or positive Clayton vine. An intercept identity and the stable VAR filter reduce the historical correction to harmonically weighted innovation moments. Terminal slope uncertainty remains in the forecast gradient. A feasible covariance estimator yields asymptotically valid repeated-sample intervals for fixed one-sided event probabilities at the realized forecast state. A same-family terminal refit provides the efficiency comparison. Retaining dated transforms adds a positive semidefinite limiting covariance term, whose event-level cost depends on dependence sensitivity and forecast-state leverage. Monte Carlo comparisons show a small accuracy cost of retaining the transforms and a larger inferential role for current marginal estimation. Allowing Clayton dependence improves downside forecasts relative to Gaussian dependence under each transform rule. A fourteen-variable U.S. real-time forecasting application and simulations with twenty and fifty variables illustrate feasible joint-event estimation and analytic inference for fixed-depth vines.

link.title: Weighted Adjoint Matching: Finetuning Flow Matching Models with Time-Dependent Control Cost

entry.content:
We introduce Weighted Adjoint Matching, a method to finetune a pretrained diffusion or flow matching model given a differentiable reward. We derive it from Adjoint Matching, which reformulates finetuning as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic control cost. Building on the observation that these models generate coarse features before fine details, we place a time-dependent weight on the control cost. A high cost early in the generative process preserves balance and diversity in the coarse features, which carry most of the semantics, while a low cost at the end lets the model increase the reward by refining details. We prove that our method is equivalent to maximizing the reward under time-varying Kullback–Leibler regularization on the generative paths. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST show a better tradeoff between reward and mode balance than Adjoint Matching.

entry.title: What Does a Discrete Diffusion Model Learn? One Reverse Process in Three Coordinates

link.title: What Does a Discrete Diffusion Model Learn? One Reverse Process in Three Coordinates

entry.content:
What does a discrete diffusion model actually learn? The literature trains denoisers, bridge plug-ins, and concrete scores, each deriving its own ELBO objective under different conventions. This fragmentation makes the object being learned unclear and ELBO values difficult to interpret and compare. All three methods learn the same object in different coordinates: the exact time-reversal of the noising process. We first prove the Oracle Distance identity: for any noising process, the negative ELBO is not just a bound on the likelihood; it equals the data entropy plus the path KL divergence from the reversed noising process to the learned one. Next, for token-factorizing noise, we show that denoiser, bridge plug-in, and concrete score are three coordinates of this reverse process, derive exact conversions between them, and identify the probability distribution learned by each. In particular, contrary to its standard interpretation, the bridge plug-in learns not a denoiser but the cavity distribution: the clean token given the noisy sequence excluding its own position. We confirm the theory by training all three coordinates with masked, uniform, and GIDD kernels on OpenWebText under a shared recipe, and by training uniform-diffusion solvers on four logic tasks. The learned coordinates agree after conversion, while confusing the cavity with the denoiser can severely degrade sampling quality. Together with exact boundary-term formulas, closed-form NELBO calibrations at initialization, and a clock interpretation of time schedules, these results provide a conceptual framework and a mechanical recipe for deriving, implementing, and comparing discrete diffusion processes.

entry.title: What If They Took the Shot? A Hierarchical Bayesian Framework for Counterfactual Expected Goals

link.title: What If They Took the Shot? A Hierarchical Bayesian Framework for Counterfactual Expected Goals

entry.content:
How would the probability of scoring change if a different player took the same shot? Although expected goals models describe the difficulty of scoring opportunities, comparing players on identical chances requires accounting for uncertainty in their estimated conversion probabilities. We address this question through a hierarchical Bayesian framework that evaluates alternative shooters under the same observed circumstances. Using 35,700 eligible shots from four leagues during the 2015/16 season, we compare a contextual benchmark with a primary player-intercept model and a provisional extension that allows player differences to vary with shooting conditions. Paired posterior draws preserve shared uncertainty when individual probability differences are aggregated across opportunities. Chronological validation demonstrates improved predictive performance relative to a constant-rate baseline, but introducing player effects provides negligible additional gains. Controlled single-seed experiments show that greater information per player improves estimation accuracy and narrows uncertainty intervals, although distinguishing small differences remains difficult and confident conclusions about near-null effects can become more frequent. Applications involving Giroud–Vardy and Berardi–Sansone similarly yield estimated differences that are small relative to their posterior uncertainty. These findings highlight an important distinction between predicting the outcome of a shot and establishing whether one player would be more likely to convert it. The proposed framework makes this distinction explicit by evaluating alternative shooters on fixed recorded opportunities while accounting for their contextual exposure. The resulting comparisons concern conditional conversion rather than the causal consequences of replacing a player in a match.

entry.summary: How would the probability of scoring change if a different player took the same shot? Although expected goals models describe the difficulty of scoring opportunities, comparing players on identical chances requires accounting for uncertainty in their estimated conversion probabilities. We address this question through a hierarchical Bayesian framework that evaluates alternative shooters under the same observed circumstances. Using 35,700 eligible shots from four leagues during the 2015/16 season, we compare a contextual benchmark with a primary player-intercept model and a provisional extension that allows player differences to vary with shooting conditions. Paired posterior draws preserve shared uncertainty when individual probability differences are aggregated across opportunities. Chronological validation demonstrates improved predictive performance relative to a constant-rate baseline, but introducing player effects provides negligible additional gains. Controlled single-seed experiments show that greater information per player improves estimation accuracy and narrows uncertainty intervals, although distinguishing small differences remains difficult and confident conclusions about near-null effects can become more frequent. Applications involving Giroud–Vardy and Berardi–Sansone similarly yield estimated differences that are small relative to their posterior uncertainty. These findings highlight an important distinction between predicting the outcome of a shot and establishing whether one player would be more likely to convert it. The proposed framework makes this distinction explicit by evaluating alternative shooters on fixed recorded opportunities while accounting for their contextual exposure. The resulting comparisons concern conditional conversion rather than the causal consequences of replacing a player in a match.

entry.title: What Information Buys in Active Inference

link.title: What Information Buys in Active Inference

entry.content:
Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF’s information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent’s data, Bayes-UCBVI’s value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent’s data, not when they are fixed.

entry.title: When Can Digital Personas Reliably Approximate Human Survey Findings?

link.title: When Can Digital Personas Reliably Approximate Human Survey Findings?

entry.content:
Digital personas powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human survey respondents, yet it remains unclear when they can reliably approximate human survey findings. We answer this question using the LISS panel, constructing personas from respondents’ background variables and pre-2023 survey histories, then testing them against the same respondents’ held-out post-cutoff answers. Across four persona architectures, three LLMs, and two prediction tasks, we assess performance at the question, respondent, distributional, equity, and clustering levels. Digital personas improve alignment with human response distributions, especially in domains tied to stable attributes and values, but remain limited for individual prediction and fail to recover multivariate respondent structure. Retrieval-augmented architectures provide the clearest gains, but performance depends more on human response structure than on model choice: personas perform best for low-variability questions and common respondent patterns, and worst for subjective, heterogeneous, or rare responses. Our results provide practical guidance on when digital personas could be appropriate for survey research and when human validation remains necessary.

entry.title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

link.title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

entry.content:
Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $\beta$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $\beta$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $\eta$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $\beta$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $\beta$ to keep $\eta/(1-\beta)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $\beta_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle’s effectiveness at a larger model scale.

entry.title: When Treatments Spill Over: A Neural Framework for Spatiotemporal Causal Effect Estimation

link.title: When Treatments Spill Over: A Neural Framework for Spatiotemporal Causal Effect Estimation

entry.content:
Real-world public health policies are often enacted by local jurisdictions, but their effects can ripple through connected populations. For causal evaluation, this creates a difficult spatiotemporal problem: intermittent policy updates create path-level treatments, and because spillover depends on neighboring treatment paths along with the focal-unit’s own history, controlling time-varying confounding requires high-dimensional, multimodal information from both sources. To address this challenge, we develop a neural spatiotemporal spillover framework that extends potential-outcome causal analysis to networked policy-systems with unit-level effects and structured interference. The framework indexes each unit’s potential outcomes through own-treatment and neighborhood spillover-exposure paths, yielding direct, spillover, and total effects. We introduce an LSTM-based representation-learning encoder that integrates each unit’s own and neighborhood histories into compact sequential summaries for downstream modeling and causal estimation. These summaries feed a self-normalized kernel inverse-probability-weighting estimator for continuous spillover exposure. Beyond theoretical guarantees, simulations show improved performance over outcome-regression baselines; in a practically motivated county-level COVID-19 policy study, the framework finds both business-and-economic restrictions and education-and-childcare policies associated with lower subsequent case burden, with larger estimates for business-and-economic restrictions. Overall, it provides a scalable, policy-interpretable framework for evaluating unit-level effects in high-dimensional, multimodal spatiotemporal systems when interventions spill over across space and time.

entry.title: Wong–Zakai Convergence and FNO Learning for Stochastic Volterra Equations

link.title: Wong–Zakai Convergence and FNO Learning for Stochastic Volterra Equations

entry.content:
This paper studies Wong–Zakai convergence and Fourier neural operator learning for stochastic Volterra integral equations (SVIEs) describing random systems with memory. A Wong–Zakai theorem establishes convergence of pathwise solutions driven by piecewise linear approximations of Brownian motion to the corresponding SVIE solution. This convergence provides a foundation for using mirror-padded Fourier neural operators to learn the solution operator mapping initial conditions and driving noise to entire solution trajectories. Numerical experiments demonstrate competitive prediction accuracy and generalization to temporal grids finer than those used for training, while assessing the influence of padding and computational cost. As a follow-up to \citet{LKP:26}, this study extends their operator-learning framework to SVIEs through separate convergence and approximation analyses tailored to convolutional memory.

entry.title: Wrong Operator or Blind Design? A Post-Training Diagnostic for Physics-Informed Coefficient Learning

link.title: Wrong Operator or Blind Design? A Post-Training Diagnostic for Physics-Informed Coefficient Learning

entry.content:
Physics-informed and hybrid models integrate data and physics, and read learned coefficients as physical. Yet a small prediction error guarantees neither that the postulated operator is right, nor that the design identifies the coefficient, nor that training reached its minimum. On one parabolic benchmark where a sensor aggregates several diffusion rates and the truth is known, a correct operator recovers the coefficient to machine precision. A wrong one leaves it $30\%$ off while the in-domain error is 1.36 times the noise, and drifts $27\%$ across windows. At $7\%$ noise the error falls below the noise; the coefficient stays $30\%$ off. Without the truth, a post-training coefficient diagnostic questions the trained model with three classical statistics, without oracle; the first two need no refit. Does it explain the data? Can the design resolve the named physics? Does the coefficient depend on the window? The specification test keeps its pre-registered false-alarm ceiling and rejects every replicate of both wrong operators tested; a network frozen at its minimum returns the same verdicts. Where the design is blind, a wrong operator confined to the unseen rate leaves the test mute; the design reading flags it beforehand. A network stopped short of its minimum mimics a wrong operator; an analytic second fit separates the two. The test has a notch against a missing reaction term, miscalibrates under correlated noise and loses power beyond $7\%$ noise. Each warning names its remedy (operator, experiment or training); silence certifies nothing.
